MOTHER ROSA GATTORNO

Foundress of the Daughters of Saint Anne

LETTERS

(1864-1870)

edited by Sr. A. Maria E. Convertini

ROME 1990 Generalate of the Daughters of Saint Anne

Ecclesiastical Approval of the Vicariate of Rome, dated 20 June 1990

PRESENTATION

The letters of Mother Rosa Gattorno, foundress of the Daughters of Saint Anne, reveal only in part the action of the Spirit in this soul wholly devoted to charity and to the love of God.

Leafing through them, one seems to be reading a family story in which worries alternate with motherly advice, all interwoven in a way that shows the mettle of the biblical woman who, though busy with the growth of her Institute, never loses sight of her own sanctification and that of her Daughters.

Every letter shows delicacy and sensitivity: one senses Mother Gattorno's involvement in life, but also her detachment from earthly cares. The letters throw light on the problems she lived with every day: Mother Rosa is practical, knows how to see and judge people and events, and readily plays down drama. Reading some of them, one seems to hear in turn the joy of a mother, the affection of a sister, the longing of a soul seeking God and trusting herself to her Directors, the sure guidance of a foundress and the devoted daughter of the Church.

Mother Rosa has a style that helps one grasp the nuances of her delicate spirit: each letter has an unmistakable vein in which one sees the moral and spiritual stature of this Woman, Foundress and Mother grow.

She becomes a discreet educator and shaper of her Daughters, using simple words, rich in spiritual and religious experience, yet aimed at the person with whom she is in dialogue. A holy emulation can be seen, enriching the holiness of the Institute's beginnings.

Most of the letters are to her Daughters: a love for them shines through every one. For each she has words of comfort, encouragement and praise: she truly feels herself a Mother and takes an interest in everything. «Bear a little more suffering for the Lord, for that good Father repays everything a hundredfold » (no. 130); «My God, steal this heart — she writes to Caterina Rapallino — so that it may pour itself out in love, for it can never find where to do so except in the centre of your heart. Saint Anne, be the guardian of that heart and shut your little Grandson Jesus inside it» (no. 6).

In the letters one feels the affectionate relationship with each Daughter come alive again: the Daughter opens herself to the Mother, and the Mother takes on the sufferings and difficulties that make the spiritual journey hard. Mother Rosa has the right word for everyone. «Courage — she writes, for example, to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa — why, now that we are on the mountain, do we lose heart at the crucifixion? Ah, no! On the contrary, we must prepare for the executioners the nails of our tribulations and long for them to be driven in soon. Come, my dear, courage, for the good Jesus will soon comfort you; he has already begun, but let us not get used to sweets, no! Let us always remember that he was given not sweet wine but gall and vinegar; so if we are to follow him, there is nothing for us but to suffer, suffer. Long live suffering! Yes, my dear, there is no softer bed to rest on than the Cross. This dear pledge holds every delight within it» (no. 80).

This excerpt from a dialogue at a distance reveals the inner richness of Mother Rosa, crucified by love, who comforts her Daughter with a page full of reflection and the fruit of spiritual wisdom and maturity. The Foundress follows her Daughters everywhere and feels and lives their problems as her own. Every day in her dialogue with God she presents her Daughters one by one, taking their burden upon herself.

But where did Mother Rosa draw such strength and courage from? A life of union with God underlies everything. Mother Rosa is a Eucharistic soul, aflame with love, whose words show how personally she feels the mystery of Christ the Redeemer, always tenderly associated with his Mother. Here is the secret of this beautiful soul: she lives within herself the joy of the cross!

Mother Rosa then expresses this inner vitality in reflections: she is a humble and wise educator, but of great moral breadth.

Every letter to her Daughters always contains points for meditation. I believe this collection can now be read with profit by everyone, and it rescues from oblivion the great riches that made Mother Gattorno a teacher in the ways of the spirit. One senses in her writing the joy of sharing her own spiritual experience: let it not be forgotten that the feelings of a tender mother grew in the foundress day by day.

Special mention should be made of the two souls who had such influence on Mother Rosa: Fr. G. B. Tornatore of the Priests of the Mission and Fr. A. Donadio of the Minims. The letters included here attest an exchange that was not bureaucratic but of great spiritual help. To Father Donadio, among other things, she wrote: «The wine of the chalice must truly keep you thirsty for you to have such a tremendous, constant burning for it. You are right to long to be drunk with it, and with all my affection I long to see you drunk with this wine» (no. 44). There was a spiritual friendship that sometimes reached the point of confidence.

Fr. Donadio was always seen in the light of the Venerable Fr. Bernardo Clausi, also a Minim, and he gladly lent himself to every request concerning the Venerable's Madonna and to furthering the newborn Institute at the Roman Curia. Such expressions of familiarity are common in the letters. «I would not want — Mother Rosa writes to Fr. Agostino Donadio — this to lead dear Father Agostino to fly like Father Bernardo's Angel; but for the love of the Lord, if that should happen, ah, come first and fetch this donkey, so that it too may share in Father Agostino's blessed flight» (no. 44).

Mother Rosa often asked for the Madonna of the Venerable Clausi and entrusted herself to her for her health and for the Institute, which was spreading more and more.

I believe Mother Gattorno's Marian devotion — bequeathed to her Daughters — was the secret of her dynamism and inner strength. She took giant strides in a crescendo of holiness that still impresses all who approach her writings today.

In these letters Mother Rosa invites us to kiss the cross, to sacrifice and to the joy of living in God. She sends a signal to people today, so poor in love, and says with consummate experience: «Let us prepare to receive the cross with open arms, for then we can better clasp it to our breast and die upon it» (no. 175).

Fr. Alessandro Galuzzi

Superior General of the Order of Minims

Rome, 14 October 1990, 159th anniversary of the birth of Mother Rosa Gattorno

INTRODUCTION

The letters of Rosa Gattorno

A source of primary importance

By their very nature as a means of communicating her thought to the sisters and to others, and by their inherent purpose, the letters of Rosa Gattorno are sources of primary importance.1 They were prompted by concrete situations and immediate needs; by her deep desire to nourish the Daughters of Saint Anne at the living source of the Institute's charism; by apostolic demands; by the sense of the Church that moved her to keep up a filial and dutiful correspondence with Church authorities; by financial needs; and by legal and administrative problems arising in the works.

With their detailed day-to-day news they lead us into the author's personal life and her varied world of relationships, extending to her religious Family and her family of origin, and to the wider social world outside, wherever she carried out her work as Foundress and Superior General of the Daughters of Saint Anne. Over the years, as the communities and their field of action multiplied, this world widened from a small regional sphere to the whole nation and to universal horizons, and became peopled with a great variety of people at work, inside and outside the Institute.2

Most notable are the still unpublished collections of her letters to friends: Fr. Agostino Donadio, Emilia di Fitalia, Cardinal Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte.

... historical

The letters are not a chronicle in the strict sense. Yet they offer a surprising quantity of material for chronicle and history. Facts, more or less significant, which, though limited to individual communities and occasional circumstances, form the warp of the Congregation's living fabric and flow into the existential weft of its tradition and history. People of the communities, and still more people of the world in which they worked, from those they cared for to collaborators, «friends and benefactors», and church and civil figures, who were themselves recipients of the part of the correspondence that may be called religious, administrative and legal. Cf. Index II and III. Exact dates — day, month, year — are also of incalculable historical value for precise knowledge of the foundations in Italy and abroad and of the whole life and development of the Institute.

... biographical

With undoubted documentary value as autobiography, they portray Rosa Gattorno's personality to the life. In her correspondence with her Daughters she makes herself known with the spontaneity of a mother who lives, speaks and acts within her family, among her own, revealing thoughts, feelings, qualities and faults, her personality and the driving energy of her tireless activity. The letters to certain friends express her rich personality, seized by an Absolute that draws every aspect of her being into unity of life, so that she is what she believes and does what she believes. Consecrated for the mission she calls «God's Work», she can only be as she is and appears, and can do only what she does, as she does it. This is the Rosa Gattorno of the letters. Beside her, reflected and as if at close range, are her correspondents. First the sisters, by spiritual, historical and numerical importance; then her children (Carlotta, Alessandro); then her closest friends, whose correspondence is remarkable in volume and quality — she wrote 356 letters to Fr. Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, 435 to Princess Emilia Labeka di Fitalia, 52 to Father Agostino Donadio — and finally many other people.

... spiritual and charismatic

Mother Rosa's letters have, and this should be stressed, a unifying centre in her very strong sense of existing for the mission: the Work

LO of God. All of them, even the most apparently insignificant, are crossed by the golden thread of her personal spiritual experience, which marked and matured her deeply. The first letter published in this opening volume, addressed to the Archbishop of Genoa, Mgr. Andrea Charvaz, contains the inspiration to found a new religious Family in the Church. Rosa Gattorno is 33, a widow with two children, already consecrated by religious vows taken privately with her confessor's consent. She belongs to the «Pious Union of the Ursulines», who took religious vows but remained with their families. She has already been refined by God's work and made fully available to his will. The call comes to the radical, all-embracing vocation of Foundress. Because of her duties as a mother towards her children she will try to clarify whether that call is genuine. But once sure that this and no other is God's will, she says her yes. The whole rest of her life unfolds from that yes. The letters, from the first, to her bishop, to the last, to a missionary Daughter of Saint Anne, revolve more or less directly around this axis: the realisation of the charism, of the spiritual intuition, in works and in a form of life; the foundation, consolidation and expansion of God's Work. She responds with complete docility to the Spirit who leads her.

... educational

There is in her a strong, compelling instinct that drives her by vocation towards the poor sick at home and in hospitals, towards girls in danger of offending against and losing their dignity as daughters of God, towards every man and woman in need. In person and through her letters she passes on to her followers the fruitful richness of her own spiritual and apostolic experience. She enlightens them with advice in the daily course of circumstances that were not always easy or favourable, so that they may live the gift consistently; she guides them in putting her charismatic intuitions into practice as concrete charity and education in faith. She seeks to form them in the original features of the Institute and in the charity that urges her from within and moves her to self-giving, in the distinctive style modelled on the Family of the holy Mother of Mary Immaculate.3 Cf. Index I.

In this respect too, then, the value of the letters is very great.

No further reasons are needed to show the value of the Foundress's correspondence and the consequent appropriateness and necessity of publishing all her letters, long felt and requested, and now desired and awaited. The aims of the work undertaken seem to us clear and achievable: to give the Daughters of Saint Anne of today and tomorrow direct contact with the Mother who shaped and formed the Daughters of her own time; to enter, through the letters, into her thought and spirit and hear again her living word in the historical, spiritual and charismatic context of her time, known so far only through the excerpts published in «Fili d'Oro»,4 precious but limited because they lack any contextual framework. Several letters have been published in «Virga Jesse», the FSA bulletin.5 Editing the whole correspondence requires not only critical study of the letters but careful, painstaking critical and methodical research into the places, situations, events and people they mention. A general knowledge of the period and its socio-cultural setting is not enough to grasp the value of the letters and interpret each one in its true sense. Long timescales are therefore unavoidable, both because of the number of documents and because of the demands of critical accuracy.

As our method we have followed a strictly chronological criterion, in blocks of years, starting from the letters concerning the foundation, without excluding or giving priority to any recipients. Volume I covers the years 1864-1870, with 273 letters.

The collection was edited by the then Superior General, Mother Celsa Speranza, who obtained from Pope Benedict XV an authoritative preface and blessing for the booklet, calling it a «florilegium of the most notable thoughts and counsels» of Mother Rosa Gattorno to her Daughters.

  • M. Rosa Gattorno nella sequela di Cristo Vergine, Virga Jesse, no. 34, 1978. 29 letters.

  • M. Rosa Gattorno alla sequela di Cristo obbediente, Virga Jesse, no. 35, 1978. 31 letters.

  • M. Rosa Gattorno nel mistero della comunione con Dio nell'orazione, Virga Jesse, no. 36, 1978. 5 letters.

By way of explanation, we offer an approach to the letters to make them easier to understand and to grasp Rosa Gattorno's original and very timely message.

With particular reference to the letters in this edition, we set out their distinctive content, their spheres and the typographical criteria, under the following headings:

  1. Biographical profile of Mother Rosa Gattorno

  2. The world of the letters - Vol. I 1864-1870 -

  3. Structure and contents

  4. Typographical criteria

1. Biographical profile

When Rosa Gattorno arrived in Piacenza on 12 March 1866 to begin a new religious Family with the five friends who had followed her from Genoa, she was 34, with a fullness of life — her great love of God and neighbour — that she sought to express in a more radical, community form of gospel living.

A woman and wife with a harmonious richness of life already lived in her family and in the sacrament of marriage, mother of children of her womb and of spiritual children, a widow for eight years, she also had behind her a fruitful, lively pastoral activity in her parish and diocese and in social service and «charity» to the sick, the poor and the needy.

Captured by God, deeply touched and enfolded by the strength and fire of his merciful love, she had given herself to him, seeking nothing but him, in doing his will, wholly given to the Work that «out of pure mercy» he entrusts to her.

Taking the foundation of the religious Family as the central event of her life, we can divide her journey into four stages, three before and one after, each intrinsically marked by growth in faith.

1831-1852 From childhood to youth

These were the years of basic preparation for the future, spent in the serene, comfortable atmosphere of a large, well-to-do family. Her father Francesco, an experienced and successful merchant in Genoa and beyond, had given the family financial security, a high standard of living and a distinguished social position. Austere, upright and honest, he brought up his children strictly and demandingly, instilling in them a noble sense of life's seriousness, love of work and tenacity of commitment to obligations undertaken, so as to bring projects to a good end. Her mother Adelaide, devout, good and gentle, was no less capable than the head of the family in devoting herself to her household and children. She had seven: one, Amalia, by her first husband, who left her a widow with a baby a few months old; and six, three boys and three girls, by Francesco. Of these Rosa, born on 14 October 1831, was the second. In this atmosphere rich in affection and values Rosa grew up serene and developed the unmistakable gifts of her personality: keen intelligence, a strong sense of realism, tenacity and firmness in her commitments, healthy affectivity, great ease of communication and capacity for deep relationships, tender love for the little ones, the defenceless and the sick, and an attraction to «the things of God».

Her mother Adelaide nurtured her dear daughter's piety, prepared her personally for first communion and saw that she received a solid Christian education through the liturgy and parish catechism.

In her family she learned the true meaning of work and of giving oneself to others, and received, besides a sound moral and Christian upbringing, the cultural accomplishments befitting her social class. Carefully chosen teachers gave her and her two sisters lessons in various subjects. She acquired a good command of Italian and French and skill in singing, drawing and embroidery. Because of her «special aptitude and rare shrewdness in the family's administrative affairs» she became her mother's adviser and friend, while her father Francesco himself shared with her his business dealings, sometimes fraught with uncertainty and risk.6

So God was educating this daughter of his, who did her best so that her mother and father, brothers and sisters, and the Father in heaven might be pleased with her. And she practised giving the best of herself, with the loving, intelligent and unconditional dedication that was her chief characteristic all her life.

The drawing room of the Gattorno house was hospitably open to family friends for visits, parties and grand receptions. But more often young intellectuals gathered there, drawn by the figure and patriotic fervour of Federico Campanella, Mamma Adelaide's «Mazzinian» brother, who had fortunately escaped capture and prison in 1833 and had returned home in 1848 after a long exile.7

Those young people, like many of their time, lived with an ideal and moral tension, seeking a new way of being and acting in a society that was changing radically. These were difficult times, as all periods of transition are, stirred by new cultural, political and social ferments. Difficult times for the Church too, which found itself assailed by the challenges of this restless society. The cultural current born of the Enlightenment, through the French Revolution, the Napoleonic aftermath and the later anti-Christian philosophies of the nineteenth century, had deeply influenced the educated classes and formed the basis of that «lay religion», often opposed to Christianity, which would be the cultural ferment from which liberalism and (in Italy) Mazzinianism developed.

To reform society and make it a paradise of justice and brotherhood was the ideal goal of these young contemporaries of Rosa Gattorno. They were moved by generous hopes, having believed in the Mazzinian utopia. Rosa, who by the age of eighteen was already taking part in family receptions as the young lady of the house, was present at the passionate discussions of these young friends. But she did not let herself be influenced. With the clear vision of Christian faith she easily saw their errors and, far from weakening or losing her faith, strengthened it and grounded it more firmly. She too was for humanity, for its cultural and moral advancement, but for humanity rooted in Christ, members of the Church, faithful to the Pope.

She stayed close to those young men, especially to her brother Federico, a convinced follower of Mazzini's ideals who later became a Senator of the Kingdom of Italy for the Republican Party; she was discreet in respecting their ideas but firm in her own convictions and Christian view of life, and faithful in begging the Lord for their conversion.

This youthful experience would strongly mark her belonging to the Church, her fidelity and love for the Pope, the Bishops and the priests, her stand in social matters, and her bold, ready answers to the challenges of her difficult times.

1852-1858 Wife and mother

One of those young men had formally asked her parents for her hand. His name was Tito Orsini, a lawyer already well established, of Mazzinian views like his brother Carlantonio, a doctor, one of the first conspirators, imprisoned in 1833. It was fortunate for her that her father Francesco decided to call off the marriage. The brilliant lawyer not only differed from the Gattornos in moral principles but was hesitant about concluding the engagement. In the book of Rosa's life another name was written as her husband.

Her cousin Gerolamo Custo had also asked for her. A deep feeling united the two young people. They felt made for each other and dreamed together of a happy life. Rosa had prepared for marriage, sure of her vocation, which had matured in prayer and discernment.

They were married on 5 November 1852 and settled in Marseilles, where Gerolamo had his business. Joy, serenity, plans for a comfortable future of assured well-being for the two of them and for the children who would come with the Lord's blessing. Happiness at being together, at that extraordinary osmosis that bound them inseparably. It was the «honeymoon». But soon this enchantment and the very certainties of their plans were sorely tested by a very hard reality: the bankruptcy of Gerolamo's business.

They tried to recover together, with faith and courage. They thought, they planned impossible solutions. But what saved them from disaster was the timely and shrewd intervention of Francesco Gattorno. Seeing that his son-in-law's good name in Marseilles was already compromised, he offered the couple generous hospitality in his own home.

Through these events Rosa thoughtfully read the presence of God the Father in her life and entrusted herself to him with the certainty of faith.

The love between Rosa and Gerolamo blossomed into new life. On 8 December 1853 Carlotta was born, and on 28 October 1855 Alessandro. Gerolamo and Rosa now had a home of their own. But towards the end of 1855, to restore the family's prosperity, Gerolamo went to Russia in business with his brother-in-law Federico.

Rosa was left alone to run the house and care for the children. Carlotta, just over two, was marked by disability: after a childhood illness she had lost her hearing — irreparably, the doctors said. With deep empathy Rosa devised a new way every day to draw her little girl out of the isolation of deafness. She gave her love and attentive communication, searching the child's face for answers, questions and signs of improvement, pursued with tireless practice, never giving up hope of a miraculous cure, begged of the Virgin with faith and tears. Alessandro, a few months old, also needed his mother.

She managed her time well. In the orderly rhythm of home life there was room too for works of «charity»: visiting the sick in hospital, caring for the needy, religious practices at home and in church. In this period she entrusted herself to the spiritual direction of Fr. Giuseppe Firpo.

In distant Ukraine, at Berdiansk, Gerolamo made good profits but, unused to northern temperatures, lost a priceless good, his health. He returned to Genoa early in 1857 in very poor condition. Another sorrow for Rosa, another call for tireless self-giving as she nursed her husband's body, weakened and damaged by illness, and his spirit, no less affected by the still more insidious malaise of discouragement, sadness and refusal to accept his condition that accompanied his physical illness, consumption.

Once again life prevailed. Serenity returned with the head of the family's apparent recovery, and the brightest hope shone again with the birth of Francesco on 1 December 1857. This new child expressed the young couple's faith in building a future and the great love that united them, drawn from the depths of God's love.

After a period of remission the illness undermining Gerolamo's health returned with such force and severity that there was no hope of recovery: pulmonary tuberculosis at a very advanced stage. Rosa stayed beside her sick husband day and night, a source of comfort and hope. Relieving his physical sufferings and the exhaustion of his worn-out body, she obtained moral strength for him from God. She guided him to rediscover in his spirit the strength of faith, cluttered over the years by many things, by money, by purely earthly plans. Now a child's simplicity resurfaced, and he prayed with his wife every day. He prayed the Hail Mary, asking for help «now and at the hour of death».

Rosa also had the children, who claimed their share of love. She did not neglect them; but the long night hours were for Gerolamo, sleepless and suffering more and more. He had asked for her heart. With her love Rosa gave him what he was unconsciously seeking most deeply: the love of God. Beside him she meditated on the drama of life and death. She entered into the mystery.8

A few months after losing her husband, her little son Francesco also died. The experience of grief was hard, but deeply formative. Here God was waiting for her, to turn her life upside down.

1858-1866 Widow

At 27 Rosa found herself with two children in her father's house, and once again he saved her from poverty. Her father's generosity and her mother's affectionate, gentle understanding moved her to deeper, grateful filial devotion, but did not give her the strength to climb out of the abyss of nothingness in which she groaned and prayed. Helped by her confessor she abandoned herself to God and found in his will peace, her true good. She entrusted herself and her children to the Virgin of Sorrows.9 Her faith now rested on God alone and became solid. Faith — she would say later — God set for me in diamond.

The crucified Saviour, whom she had implored beside the bed of her Gerolamo, consumed by tuberculosis and himself crucified, now bent over her poverty and revealed to her how far he had loved her, had loved every human being. It was her conversion.

Her life changed. She saw, heard and touched the inexpressible reality of the invisible. She prayed at length, night and day, wore hair shirts, fasted. She had a Spouse of her soul: Christ Crucified. She bound herself to him by vows of poverty, chastity and obedience and set out with him. Only Calvary — she writes — I know to be the safe place to stop.10

To Carlotta and Alessandro were added other children, many of them: the sick, the

poor, «endangered» girls, children to be taught the faith. She cared for her parents and the house. But she also had another house to turn to: the church, dwelling of her Good and meeting place of her brothers and sisters in faith.

She lived for the Spouse, for him alone, ready to suffer «every pain and death itself». To the poor she, poor herself, gave herself, her time, attention and labour, and what little food — meat, bread, fruit — she could deftly set aside from her own meals. She spent hours on end in church, absorbed in Eucharistic contemplation or in pastoral work: works of zeal (as they were then called), catechesis, spreading good literature; and in social work: seeking out girls «at risk» or «in danger», that is, alone, far from their families because of work, exposed to hardship and danger; visiting and nursing the sick poor at home and in hospital.

Meanwhile the unification of Italy was taking place under the banner of anticlericalism, while the dechristianising movement begun beyond the Alps was subtly penetrating the educated circles of Italian cities. The Church, under attack, suffered as an institution, since it had to defend economic and political power as a guarantee of its autonomy and freedom. But perhaps precisely through this apparent loss it gained as a community of believers. It was reborn, one might say, more alive in its many institutions of piety and charity, in a renewal that came from the people.

In Genoa, as elsewhere, new religious and social associations and institutions were founded by zealous priests.11 Rosa Gattorno took an active part in some of them, above all the «Pious Union of the Daughters of Mary Immaculate» and the «Pious Association for the Preservation and Growth of the Catholic Faith». Through instructions and conferences she deepened and enriched her religious knowledge and committed herself fully to the «works of mercy» prescribed for members. The Daughters of Mary Immaculate, among other things, nursed the poor sick women of the area; for «the preservation and growth of the Catholic faith» members promoted through specific works «the instruction of youth in Christian doctrine», supported «continual adoration of the Blessed Sacrament» and undertook «the protection of girls whose morals were in danger».12

They worked and tackled problems with the practical, organisational sense typical of the Genoese. Among other things, a special Commission was set up expressly to deal with the serious problem of girls in danger. Rosa Gattorno was appointed Vice-President, and in this field she showed what a woman of strong character and strong faith could do. She was tireless in seeking out, helping and comforting the girls with a mother's tact and understanding. She had uncommon organisational gifts. She was a great heart that spent itself more each day for everyone, and she had a quiet, fascinating influence over the Genoese ladies who, like her, devoted themselves to charity. She became a point of reference.

She had come a long way on the spiritual path. Her first biographer, Fr. A. M. Fiocchi, writes: «In the course of four years (1858-1861) this soul had climbed so high in self-purification and union with Christ that the quick accents of her aspirations have the style of the great saints and savour of the folly of the cross».13 This judgement confirms what Fr. Firpo wrote to Rosa for her consolation: «You no longer are; you no longer live; it is your Spouse Jesus, your love, your all who lives and works in you... you must serve him only as a poor instrument, as you are».14

But something happened that was to be of great importance in her life. Fr. Giuseppe Frassinetti had resolved to give the «Pious Union of the Daughters of Mary Immaculate» the form of a true religious Congregation and had written its Rule. To speed up the Archbishop's long-delayed approval, he asked for Rosa Gattorno's help.

Mgr. Charvaz received her personal request and, somewhat puzzlingly, asked her to guess what he considered unsuitable in that Rule. She, without asking awkward «whys» and without excuses or resistance, discreetly withdrew, taking the pages to examine.

She sank into prayer before the Crucifix. Inspired, she marked the passages of Frassinetti's Rule that did not please the Archbishop. She prayed again. Then, during prayer, she also wrote on a slip of paper a small outline of the Regulations of another Congregation that might be founded and, without realising the import of what later circumstances revealed to be a true inspiration, she kept the sheet.

But the small seed of life disturbed and unsettled her. She spoke of it to her spiritual director, Fr. Firpo, and was firmly ordered to present the plan to the Archbishop. She obeyed and went. She was convinced that, given her many commitments in the diocese and above all her duties to her children, someone else could carry out the work. Instead she felt called to act personally, she and no other. But the irresistible strength of maternal love found, in the face of her Pastor's authority, a way out by appealing to a higher authority. She would go to the Pope; he, she thought, would release her from this impossible obligation, contrary to the spirit of the holy Gospel.

1866-1900 Foundress and Superior General

Pius IX, instead, encouraged her and ordered her to carry out that inspiration. It was God's will. Rosa Gattorno understood. She suffered unspeakably for her children. Once again she entrusted them to the Virgin of Sorrows. She grieved for her elderly parents. In prayer she found again the strength for the road «to Calvary». The Work was God's, not hers. And for God's Work she offered herself as a victim, firmly resolved to offer everything and suffer everything for it.16

Particular circumstances led her to begin the Work in Piacenza. Ready to do God's will in everything and at any cost, she felt that he wanted her there and that she must leave all security: her parish, her diocese, her family, her friends, her whole Genoese world. Having cut her ties at the root, she set out with five companions. In Piacenza, after a provisional start in a rented house, the little group found its community home in the Palazzo Dal Verme, bought with money lent to her by one of the five companions, Teresa Porta, widow Morasso.17 The building was large and had to be adapted to the group's needs. It would be the Lord's house. Its heart and centre was the little chapel, the point of light of their new life. The Blessed Sacrament was reserved there, a privilege the Foundress had already obtained in Rome. The rooms needed for the time being were furnished with the utensils, furniture, beds, mattresses and linen brought by the new residents.18 Rosa chose for herself the smallest, most remote little room and made it her hermitage. It was the place of intimate encounters, prolonged day and night in prayer and penance with her crucified Good. It was the womb of the family the Father would give her as a life-giving gift of immense love.

The rhythm of life was sober and strict: prayer, daily Eucharist, silence, work, study, and charity through home visits to the sick poor. They went in pairs. The people of Piacenza, admiring their dignity and composure, called them the Genoese ladies. At first they had no uniform habit. Their inspiring model was the early Christian community: one heart and one soul. The central figure was Rosa Gattorno, whom all loved, esteemed and regarded as Mother.

A priest from Cremona, Fr. Luigi Cogrossi, whom they had all known before going to Piacenza, gave the little family spiritual care and advice and celebrated the Eucharist for them every day.19

The Mother guided, taught, directed and acted, but not arbitrarily. She let herself be guided by the Spirit, the «Governor». Before speaking she waited for the Father's «prompting». In acting she drew inspiration from the obedience and the measure of love of Christ Crucified, her Good. Measured against that standard, what she gave and did always seemed little to her. Like a poor «donkey» she let the Eternal Father load her burden on her, never saying «enough», and went on, leading the others above all by example.20

Life, of course, was not easy. Of the first five, three did not feel able to continue on the path begun with her and went back home. But the Father gave her other daughters.21 She welcomed with joy and trepidation their opening to the new life of her Crucified Good, and spent on them all the treasures of full life contained in her womanly personality: gifts of intelligence and intuition, springs of spiritual energy, the ability to listen, to welcome and to relate, life experience, aspirations. And a heart so poor and so centred on God that it opened freely to the gift of love of her dear Eternal Father and of her Good. In short, the gift of the founding charism.

A significant coincidence: in the same period in which that charism was taking shape, the Parliament of the Kingdom of Italy decreed, on 14 May 1866 (law 3036), the suppression of all religious Orders and Congregations and the confiscation of their property, extended by the later law of 19 June 1873 (no. 1402) to the former territories of the Papal State, which had become part of the Kingdom with the occupation of Rome (1870).

This unjust and arbitrary law nevertheless opened, in God's plans, the way to a wonderful renewal in the decades that followed. «A purer, younger Church is born, which has lost its former political power but has intensified its spiritual action».22 The living forces of this renewal were the new forms of religious life that flourished. Under the pontificate of Pius IX as many as 40 congregations arose, among them the religious Family of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Rosa Gattorno's call, through the explicit will of Pius IX, belongs in precisely this context: a very particular call to special consecration and mission, whose scope and lines of action, listening to the Spirit, she expressed day by day, as these letters clearly document.

- a mission expressed in the gift of motherhood:

  • to give birth to daughters in the spirit, nourish them with the «delicious milk» of the teaching of the incomparable Master, Jesus the Saviour, and direct and guide them to the sublime holiness to which he calls them in the Family of the holy Mother of the Immaculate.

  • To teach them to grasp, through the deep, intimate bond between her, the Mother, and them, the Daughters, the unity of them all as sisters born in Saint Anne to the divine love that flows through the Family.

  • To form true Daughters of Saint Anne through the spoken word, writings, visits to the communities and, above all, witness. To go before them all in observing the Rule, «the sure way to become holy and not stray».

  • To nourish them in love for the sublime mission to which God calls them: to sanctify themselves and help their neighbour to holiness, moved solely by the love that seeks to please God. A

motherly, unconditional love for one's neighbour that does not shrink from giving one's own life in humble service «of charity».

This last stage of the Mother's life is the longest: 34 years. With the gift for synthesis that came from concentrating on and living the essential, she sums it up in the main features of her work as foundress and superior general. «My life was constantly travelling about, now for founding houses, now for begging, so as to support the sisters, and of it all I make an offering to God of my sufferings, and shut up in Him his poor slave lived (if it could be called having life), for only my Master, my all, I can assure you, led me like a little girl».23

The final stage marks the summit of her human and theological maturity. Unified in a single centre — God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit — and following the maternal models of Mary and Anne, she fulfils the mission of bringing to birth in the Church a religious Family that expresses the features of God's face in the maternal traits of love: mercy, the gentle and deep tenderness of motherhood.

She is moved by the sufferings and poverty of God's children, bends over each one and serves each freely and simply, in the discreet anonymity that belonged to Saint Anne.

It is impossible to measure the fruits of Rosa Gattorno's self-offering in God's Work, for in the economy of grace there are no human yardsticks. Yet a few figures can give, in the visible order, some idea of how fruitful it was. When she was called to the Father's house on 6 May 1900, aged 69, the Institute had spread like the flight of a dove, as Pius IX had prophesied, in Italy and abroad, and numbered more than 4,000 sisters and 368 communities.24

2. The world of the letters 1864-1870

Compared with the whole correspondence, which from 1864 to 1900 reaches a great many recipients in many different settings, this collection may seem an insignificant part because of its chronological limits, since the letters in fact belong to the four years 1864-1870. Only two are from 1864, one from 1865, two from 1866. The number too is relatively small: 273 letters out of more than

9,000, and the recipients number little more than thirty. Yet this correspondence has a special importance that comes not from external assessments but from its inner, germinal dimension, bursting with dynamic vitality, in the historical and spiritual role of the first implantatio of God's Work, the new seedling being born in the Church. We are at the beginning, in the years when the Foundress's inspiration was gradually taking shape in its distinctive practical aspects, and the first followers, who also shared in the gift, were growing, enlightened and guided by the Mother, in awareness that they were not only followers, disciples and daughters but fellow workers in the community, sharing in different ways in running the Work and jointly responsible for the life and holiness of the whole Family. And they were building unity among themselves around their pivot, the Mother, who inspired them all with her ardent charity and her example.

Historical importance

The letters give us above all reliable information on the opening and activity of the first communities, and on the closure of some of them.

  • At Cento (Ferrara) the community began nursing the sick in a hospital (February 1867). This work ended in the spring of 1869.

  • At Piacenza, the Mother House, they took in:

  • the orphans of cholera victims, giving them a home, food and an all-round education;

  • later, «endangered» girls

  • deaf-mute girls, who therefore needed specialised teaching (Lett. 36, 37, 38).

  • At Sampierdarena (Genoa) another community devoted itself (1868) to elementary schooling for poor girls and boys, the formation of girls in a boarding school, and home nursing of the sick.

  • In the same period some Sisters from this community worked in an institute in Genoa opened by a priest, taking charge of its direction, schooling and the formation of the boarding girls.

- Another community started a boys' school for poor boys in Piacenza (1870). Cf. Index IV.

They also give news of plans to open other works — at Parma, Pieve di Cento, Cerro Maggiore (MI), Milan — which were not carried out, or were carried out later, as at Nizza Monferrato.

In the manner proper to family correspondence, they take the place of the chronicles, which did not exist in those first years and began only later. They show the way of life, the poverty and the resourceful ways of earning at least the bare minimum each day: sewing, knitting, embroidery, weaving, begging, raffles and exhibitions show how the work went on. People, events and circumstances inside and outside, relations with collaborators, administrators, friends and... enemies. A whole reality seen through the eyes and heart of the Foundress and interpreted by her with faith as she told it to the daughters she wrote to.

They portray life as it was being lived in its new evangelical, community and apostolic form. The protagonists: the Mother, the sisters, those they cared for. Figures in the foreground and background appear and speak the existential language of love and pain, of living and dying, of courage and discouragement. And they reappear in the ups and downs of daily life.

The Mother is a constant presence, central in her creaturely reality, called to so great a task. Strong in spirit but physically very weak and in poor health, she lives poverty and constant travel in imitation of her divine Master. And with the Mother, the sisters. Those closest to her, who share the responsibility of government as her most direct collaborators: Francesca Camisa and Adelaide Pezzoni, both superiors, and Vincenza Rapallino, first secretary, who received most of the letters. And the others, who held various offices in the communities, also loved, followed and valued with great love.

The life expressed and recounted in the letters is the response to the call and mission that the new religious Family was carrying out in the most varied circumstances, with loving attention to God's design in his Work, to the pole of his will, and under the dynamic impulse of the Holy Spirit.

Spiritual importance

The letters also raise the curtain on a spiritual reality no less beautiful, fascinating and varied. Above all they reveal the Mother in her deepest inner space. She presents herself, in the facets of her rich and complex personality, with her characteristic spontaneity, to her daughters and confidantes. She expresses her thoughts about God, people, things and events. She reveals the wisdom of her Christian experience, her moods, her motherliness, which becomes active, industrious goodness.

We know from other sources (the Memoirs) the life of contemplative intimacy and the mystical gifts with which she was favoured, which she jealously kept secret between herself and her Good. Yet the letters give us glimpses of her intimacy with the Lord in the spontaneous prayers that welled up from her heart in the midst of her dialogue with her daughters, placing herself and them in the warm current of Trinitarian love. Or they tell how to speak to the Lord, how to live in his presence (L. 20, 141), how to stand before him in happy or sad situations (L. 82), easy, hard or dangerous, and in the most varied settings (L. 92), how to abandon oneself to his love, following his voice and will (L. 82), how to run swiftly on the way of holiness (L. 70), with what intensity of love to embrace the cross and clasp it to one's breast, «a treasure the world does not know, which (Jesus) offers to his beloved spouses» (L. 7), as a pledge of «eternal joy after brief suffering».

The letters clearly highlight the Foundress's specifically maternal role in the mysterious process of constantly giving life and making room to receive life. A self-giving relationship with her daughters, mediated by the vertical relationship with God. A tender, sincere, intense affection, made still more radical and absolute by the love of God that pervades her (L. 37, 147, 148, 213). It becomes a source of theological comfort in faith, hope and charity, a fruitful dynamism of «edification» which, in the I-thou relationship, widens within the community and from there outwards into a wider world of relationships.

Indirectly, they shed light on the inner world of the happy and fortunate sisters inspired by the Mother's presence, and on the spiritual life of those first fervent communities, where one breathed harmony, gospel simplicity, industry and love.

...and charismatic

Most of these letters, whether to individual sisters or to communities, are formative. They continue, clarify and complete the educational work the Foundress carried out in personal and community meetings.

Her spiritual experience and awareness of the charismatic gift gave rise in the Mother, as a particularly strong impulse, to a sense of her responsibility to educate her Daughters in a distinctive spirit. A cross-reading of the letters brings out:

  • her personal experience of God, her thinking on discipleship, her imitation of Christ and sharing in his saving mission;

  • her spiritual journey.

These are the cornerstones of the founding gift she is called to hand on in the maternal and teaching role inherent in it. From them comes the unmistakable richness of content and educational guidance in the process of formation:

- Jesus' call in the family of the holy Mother has precise marks of discipleship: «see, whoever wishes to follow me, says the Master (showing us the cross), let him take up his cross and follow me... He gives me that treasure which the world does not know and which he offers to his beloved spouses, and even sees to it that it is heavy, so that one day we may come to taste his delights» (L. 7).

How to respond to the gift? The Mother puts her daughters through a school of life:

- «Let us throw ourselves into the bosom of the Eternal and beg him to do with us what he wills» (L. 7).

«To become holy and always do the dear will of God, the sole object of our thoughts» (L. 6).

«To find true joy in the adversities and crosses that Jesus sends us and, as Master, teaches us. If we want to learn this, we must keep this mirror, the figure of the Redeemer, before our eyes and continually look at our own figure in him. With so true a model, I assure you, everything comes to fit us perfectly. To keep him always present, so as to attune the mind to such sublime teachings for true holiness, practising that charity which I so much recommended and which our M. Saint Anne teaches us» (L. 20).

«To make new and ever living resolutions of love and constancy in wanting to follow him, and always to carry them out» (L. 11).

«Jesus is the dear one of your heart, the being of your every thought; all that we do, all is for Jesus» (L. 15).

«Take comfort, you who labour for your Jesus. You are always conversing with Jesus, because in touching those sick people with charity, and with the great charity that your dear Mother Saint Anne had... In those sick creatures Jesus is found» (L. 11).

«Blessed are you when that day comes and you can say: I am dying because I wore myself out too much in works of charity. Then be sure that dear Mamma Saint Anne will be waiting for you at the gates of Paradise, to receive you blessed and holy for eternity» (L. 11).

«My dears, you have the means to become very holy, and holy quickly» (L. 11).

A sure means of fulfilling the call to holiness in the Family of the holy Mother is the Rule: «Remember often why you became religious. Answer: to become holy. So if that is what you want, read often the book you carry in your pocket and try to imprint it on your heart and mind, so as to observe exactly all it contains, and God will help you put it into practice, and by this means you will become holy» (L. 128).

The precious little book was the formation text the sisters had to know, absorb and live. The Mother explained its contents assiduously, aiming to form «those creatures whom Saint Anne desires, observant of the Rule, from the moment they open their eyes in the morning until evening, overcome by sleep» (L. 117, 142, 184, etc.).

Observance is the condition of true life for the Family of the holy Mother, an open door to Providence and to peace (L. 139). Focal points she presses with insistent recommendations:

  • Obedience, the path of radical discipleship: «obey, if you want to be holy» (L. 123).

  • Prayer, «the compass that leads to the pole, to the centre that is God. Take care always to keep your thoughts turned to God and to see everything in him» (L. 8).

- Silence, the personal inner climate of life in God (L. 147) and the community climate that fosters growth in virtue and harmony (L. 141).

In observance she went before them all and was an exemplary model: «daughter, have you ever seen this poor Mother of yours stray from the least of the holy Rules?» (L. 194).

Against failures of observance she had words of fire (L. 178).

Mother Rosa's awareness of the gift is very clear. She writes to Sr. Adelaide Pezzoni, who had told her of her difficulties in her new task as superior: «See to what sublime greatness (the Redeemer) has raised you, to take an active part in a new Order of his being born in the bosom of his beloved spouse. One day we shall know in all its extent the worth, the power, the eternal glory for those who have had a part in it. All this we shall see in the glory of the blessed...» (L. 157).

The «great Work which in time we shall see flourish throughout the Catholic and anti-Catholic world» (L. 226) was entrusted to her poor shoulders, to her «labouring for Jesus and for the dear, dear Eternal Father» (ibid.). And she did not spare herself. «I thank you infinitely for the prayers you say for my health, and believe me, when the Lord gives me a little, I spend it at once for the good of Saint Anne's house, like the Eternal Father's poor donkey, which, when it feels a little strength, knows nothing else to do but carry the load its God puts on its shoulders» (L. 117). But she also takes on her daughters' burden: «answer me that you will embrace your cross... I will say to Jesus: give my little daughter the lighter part and the heavier part to me» (L. 183).

The letters document the strength of her love and toil in clearing, planting and cultivating the «vast field and delightful garden of the Redeemer gardener» (L. 157), so that true Daughters of Saint Anne might be born. For them, her whole life, her labours, her time. «This poor Mother of yours has nothing else in mind but your holiness...» (L. 128). With the liveliest hope, foreseeing that «eternal joy» in Paradise which God in his mercy — so she hopes — will grant to her and her daughters beside the holy Mother (L. 220).

The eschatological dimension touched on here is one of the dominant elements of Mother Rosa's spirituality. The letters show the measure of the Mother's theological life and of her being centred on her Crucified Good, sharing in his suffering, «my only joy, my only treasure» (L. 181), which wins us joy among the blessed in the heavenly Homeland (L. 209).

There is only one goal. And towards it she leads her Daughters, inspiring them with her own ardour. «Courage! A brief suffering for a great joy» (L. 237) is her most frequent exhortation, full of hope, with different reasons according to circumstances. «Jesus always drives strong souls forward by dint of spurring, until they have reached Golgotha and there, crucified with him, they may rise again all beautiful and shining and enter in triumph into the glory of heaven» (L. 239).

3. Structure and content of the letters

Almost all the letters in this collection are autographs. Their structure is simple. The place followed by the date, usually at the top right or, more rarely, at the bottom left at the close of the letter. The characteristic greeting, abbreviated A.M.F. (Anna, Maria, Francesco), at the top left. From April 1869 (L. 114) comes the greeting prescribed by the 1869 Rule, Ch. 12, 3: «Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne», preceded by another greeting, used on Fr. Tornatore's advice: «The blessing of our Eternal Father be with us». Usually, between the two greetings, comes the salutation, more or less varied but affectionate: dear daughter; dear superior; my dear daughter... (name of the recipient); my (name), dear to Jesus; dear to Jesus and my beloved superior. In particular circumstances the affectionate expression is more tender and expressive: my dear, mine forever, beloved daughter [...]; my good superior, blessed daughter; our daughter and mine, in all and through all; our daughter and wholly ours. Often, from the end of 1869, the salutation uses the plural our, in deference to Father Tornatore, whom she regarded as Co-founder and Superior.

Then comes the body of the letter, of very varied length: from several pages to a few lines.

The closing is brief but intense and expressive. The signature is preceded by simple, terse phrases: your most affectionate Mother; your most affectionate, poor Mother; poorest Mother.

Often a postscript or a note follows, expressing recommendations, warnings, forgotten thoughts or repeated reminders.

The style is frank, spontaneous, intensely expressive. But the thought is not always expressed in a clearly and logically structured sentence, and it can be obscure, partly because the punctuation is generally careless. There are at times misspellings, dialect idioms and grammatical slips. Free of any stylistic striving, Mother Rosa writes in ordinary spoken language, except in letters to persons in authority, which reflect the formal, emphatic bureaucratic style of the nineteenth century. This aspect, though marginal, reveals the underlying culture that runs through the whole correspondence.

A daughter of her time, belonging to the upper class of a city open to innovations and fashions from beyond the Alps, Rosa Gattorno had absorbed through study the customs, tastes and manners of the age, the Romantic culture of her time. Its prominent aspects, the religious and sentimental strand, touched her sensibility and inspired her to do great things for the ideal, which for her was the call to spend herself wholly and always for God's Work. Her immediacy is the heroic-romantic expression of her dynamic, realistic and practical personality, which sometimes leads her to use terms borrowed from the patriotic language of the period, in a triumphalist vein to which the church language of the time was, after all, no stranger.

She is quick in thought, as in putting inspirations into practice and carrying them through with resolve and courage. She uses verbs of great energy. «Look at Peter. Come, said the Master, and he, without thinking that he had a family and other things, ran at once. Certainly this Master was not out for a stroll or for pleasures, but was ready for anything, to leap hedges, climb through forests... in search of the lost sheep» (L. 7). «So, courage on the Lord's way... this is the only way to run safely on the road that leads safely to heaven» (L. 231).

No evasions, no time to lose. She makes use of time, treasuring every moment to write to her daughters. «I take advantage of every moment» (L. 161). From her father's house, where she had gone because of her illness, she writes: «The doctor and all the others are around the bed, so I am using these minutes to answer you» (L. 179). «I am writing in several sittings» (L. 128); «this is the fourth time I have taken it up again» (L. 226). As soon as possible, any place will do for a letter-dialogue with her daughters: «Read as best you can, for I am writing in haste on a corner of a table» (L. 106). «My dear, I am writing to you on a bench (stool) by the looms, sitting almost on the floor, with their noise deafening me» (L. 132).

Her style is affected not only by lack of time and less than ideal surroundings but also by her health: «Just two lines, because it is very late and I am not well» (L. 126). «Though it is late and I am very tired, this evening too I want to devote a little rest to you, my dear ones» (L. 7).

She usually keeps the evening for correspondence, and the small hours arrive. But when she writes she does not notice time passing. Sometimes «I am sleepy» slips out (L. 30), but she goes on writing. At other times she really does stop. «I will not go on, because my head aches and I feel unwell» (L. 123). These and similar phrases express simplicity and freedom, a climate of spontaneous confidence and family trust.

When she speaks of God or the spiritual life she is carried away by the rush of feeling and does not always manage to express her thought clearly. A small correction would be enough to put it right. But she rarely rereads what she has written. She writes as her heart dictates, or rather, all that her Good wants her to say.

She forcefully expresses deeply rooted convictions, drawn from religious experience in «the Master's sublime school», and often repeats them across a rich range of themes.

Her letter-writing style shows a gift for personal relationship, welcome, understanding and empathy. When advising the sisters she sometimes suggests the very words they should say. When making suggestions she anticipates their answers or objections: «You will tell me..., but I shall answer you...».

In their marked simplicity the letters show the underlying climate of the spiritual and affectionate relationships with which the Mother nourished her daughters in the pure love of God, even when dealing with purely practical, routine matters.

They present a range of varied content: spiritual instruction in the more strictly formative ones; news of Family life, information, reports; directions about the works and dealings with people; exhortations, encouragement or rebukes; notices of arrivals, departures and consignments (cloth, flour, clogs for the girls, etc.); receipt of letters; travel accounts; exchanges of news about the health of the Mother and the sisters; instructions for jobs to be done in the house; errands for purchases, delivery of letters or goods. A whole ferment of activity, lived in constant harmony with the divine.

4. Criteria for this edition

The letters in this edition belong to the period 1864-1870. They are published in a standard scholarly edition, directly from the autograph originals kept in the Historical Archive of the Daughters of Saint Anne, Generalate, Rome.

To guarantee textual fidelity for the reader, only strictly necessary changes have been made: punctuation, capitals or lower case, double consonants. One or more words missing from the text but needed to understand the Mother's thought have been added in [ ], while original words of the text that make exact understanding difficult have been placed in ( ).

To make each letter easier to read and to present it in a clearer typographical form, the text has been divided into consecutively numbered paragraphs. This also allows citations to be precise, as explained below.

The letters are dated in chronological sequence. Where the original bears no date, we have fixed the most likely one on the basis of internal and external evidence, placing it in [ ].

Each letter is introduced by a very brief «regestum» and accompanied by explanatory notes of a historical, psychological, spiritual, scriptural and charismatic nature.

Where only a person's first name or, conversely, only the surname appears in the text, it has been completed in the relevant note. Personal details of people named in several letters are generally given in a note at their first appearance, while related events concerning them are given progressively in the notes to the individual letters. The notes therefore also contain cross-references to other letters, so that the most notable and significant historical events of the Institute in this first period of its existence can be followed in parallel.

é

In citing the letters, the serial number identifying them in this collection is given, followed by the paragraph number if the citation refers to the text (e.g. L. 1, 2). If it refers to a note, the letter number is followed by the abbreviation n (e.g. L. 1,n2).

The fundamental and characteristic themes of Mother Rosa's spirituality are listed by entry in analytical index I. Drawn from the general content of the letters, they highlight the distinctive aspects of her spirituality and are thus a reference source for study and deeper knowledge. Each entry refers to the letter of origin, marked by its number in the collection in bold, followed by the numbers of the paragraphs containing the entry concerned (e.g. L. 1, 1, 2, 4).

Then comes index II, of the recipients of the letters published, with brief biographical notes.

Completing it is index III, of notable persons named in the letters whose presence affected the life of the Institute.

Finally, index IV gives essential historical outlines of the foundations made from 1866 to 1870, the period illuminated by this first block of letters. Together with the two previous indexes, it offers a clearer, more coherent overall view and general frame of reference for understanding the letters as a whole, and helps in the exact interpretation of individual letters and of groups related in content and purpose.

Account of the inspiration received concerning the rule for founding a new religious Congregation.1

Most Reverend Excellency,

I make it my duty to send you what you commanded me the last time I had the grace of speaking with you in person.

Monastic Rules for the Daughters of the Immaculate, the Minims of Saint Francis of Assisi.

1. Annual vow of chastity

2. Vow of obedience

3. Vow of poverty

4. Unmarried young women and widows will be admitted; after a year of probation, if they have a vocation, the Superior will admit them to profession. They are then to work for the increase of our holy Faith and for the care of the sick in their homes, and they will also take in girls at risk,2 whom they will teach Christian doctrine and needlework.

5. To the sick whom they nurse, if they are poor, they will bring something they need, and everything will be free. From the rich they will accept an offering for the monastery.

6. Each candidate will bring to the monastery whatever her family can give, according to their means, since all must live in perfect community and poverty, and work only for the poor and for poor churches.

7. They will have special obligatory prayers. Morning and evening they will make some prayer in common, such as meditation. The Superior will arrange that all may receive Holy Communion daily, always, however, with the confessor's consent.

8. The habit will be very simple, black and of wool. 9. Their food will be meatless, with dairy products. If any of them suffers from the meatless diet, the Superior will have her eat meat.

Here, Your Excellency, is a poorly ordered sketch of the Rules I would give to the future Daughters of the Immaculate.

[... Signed Maria Rosa Gattorno]

So let us not deceive ourselves: in the Lord's works patience and sacrifice are needed.34 God is more pleased with sacrifices than with great promises or anything else.5 Jesus sacrificed himself for us and drank the bitter cup to the last evening, and we grieve so much at being far away rather than near. Ah! Come, my little ones, let us throw off our swaddling clothes, cast ourselves into the bosom of the Eternal and beg him to do with us what he wills.6 Yes, dear ones of Jesus, courage and firm constancy, and with this you will see God's help; whereas always wanting to put in our own contribution is a way of driving God's workings away from us.

When his apostles wanted the children kept away from him, Jesus said: no – Jesus replied – let the children come to me! What does this mean? All who go to Jesus stripped of every will of their own, and are not so finicky in their observing, thinking themselves able to discern, but – let us really run to the Master to learn everything, with the simplicity of children – these will find a place to rest in his bosom.7

All dejected, because we see ourselves wrapped in our littleness, in rags on every side, trembling, we no longer know how to call the Spouse, for he is all beautiful and we are misshapen.
