Dear Superior,

  1. Just two lines to answer your dear letter. For now I cannot answer my dear girls, but I will as soon as I can; indeed I am busy composing a little prayer.1

  2. Then I would like Daria and the others, when they write to me, to write separately and hand the letter to you sealed, so that they can tell me what is in their hearts more openly.2

  3. I also want you to keep the month of Saint Anne, which you will certainly have begun.3 Pray, dear Superior: prayer is the only weapon to defend ourselves against so many insidious dangers.

  4. Write to me at once. I recommend humility and the observance of the Rules to you. Today we have exposition.4 Fr. Luigi still in Rome.5

Greet everyone for me, the doctor's wife6 and everyone. Goodbye,

I am your most loving Mother Rosa

She describes Carlotta's first communion celebration in Milan. She instructs all the Sisters on the theological life in the charitable service of the sick and in community life.

A.M.F.

Dear Superior,

  1. Just two lines, because I am so busy that I cannot stay long with you, and still more because of my poor health, which always makes me fail in every duty. Today I suffered a great deal, because I went to visit a sick woman who lived very far away, so I leave you to imagine what such a long outing did to me.

  2. I went to Milan on the 4th of this month to see Carlottina make her communion.1 I left Piacenza at three in the morning and reached Milan at ten to five. There I went to a church to receive Communion, and at half past six I went to the school. Dear Superior, what can I say: it pleased the Lord that when I came out of the school I was seized by such a violent headache that, as soon as I reached my sister-in-law's house, while everyone was at the communion ceremony, I had to go to bed, suffering horribly. At twelve my mother2 went to fetch the girl and brought her to me. But no! I got up, but was soon lying down again, practically on a sofa, and dear Carlottina insisted on staying beside me the whole time until five, when the pain eased somewhat. We went to table, and afterwards my sister-in-law took the girl back to the school, and my mother, Caterina3 and I returned to Piacenza, arriving at 11 at night. They fumigated us; my dear, we thought we would die; Caterina, with the breathlessness she suffers from, was choked by such a stench. It was enough to kill you.

  3. Now settled in Piacenza, but there is a world of things to sort out and then, as you know, the Exercises.4 I thought it best that you should come for the feast of Saint Francis.5

  4. I was sorry to keep hearing the story about the broth, but you must not mind it, since the Bursar tastes it every day; enough: to live securely and in peace, ask the Bursar from time to time whether it is all right, and pay no attention to the rest.

  5. Tell the girls that I always mean to send them a little keepsake, but I have no time and do not know how to manage it.

  6. Fr. Luigi6 has not come yet; here we enjoy a paradise of peace, everything goes with perfect exactness; I hope it is the same there.

  7. They will love one another with one heart and always mirror themselves in their Spouse Jesus, to see in him the model they must conform to; that is, in order to practise the evangelical charity of our Redeemer and dear and holy humility. Ah! my Sisters and daughters, for charity's sake keep yourselves very low, if you want one day to be great in Paradise, the one goal of all our labours.7 Yes, my Jesus, no other motive leads us to live this life but your love. One day to see you and enjoy you face to face: that is our glory, that is everything. Yes, I tell you, dear daughters, our centre, our happiness! Ah! To have this, as you well know, nothing else is needed but to despise everything that belongs to the world and to see and live everything for Jesus.

  8. Often remember to imitate the charity of your Mother Saint Anne.8 True charity towards one's neighbour. To love those who suffer, to suffer with them, to love one another with one heart, and your Superior as Jesus, because you must see her in the figure of your Spouse. So imagine: if he gave you orders, what obedience would you not show? Well, he commands you through your Superior.

  9. Courage, my dears, pray much, laugh little, always try to keep to yourselves; pray much and meditate a great deal, for you always have the means to meditate: seeing Jesus in the sick, how easy you will find meditation on the passion of Jesus!9

10. My Superior, do you perhaps need anything? Please write and tell me, and I will do all I can at once to send you what you want.

Goodbye, dear daughters. God bless you, and you, Superior, believe me always your Mother Rosa

She answers the letters received and gives news. Suggestions about the bursar. She sends greetings and asks for news of various people.1

A.M.F.

My Superior, dear to Jesus

  1. Here I am with you to answer all your dear letters. It is all over; our celebrations went marvellously2 and when I come I will tell you everything.

  2. How it pains me not to be sure that what I write to you will not be read! May the will of Jesus be done, the beginning and end of all we do!

  3. As you know, my health gets worse from one day to the next; indeed during the novena of our dear Mother I was in bed, you might say, for six days. Now I am up, but only just; the swelling, you know, keeps getting worse.

  4. Let us leave these gloomy thoughts and come to you, dear Superior. You did not understand what I said about the Bursar in my last letter. I wanted, first, that at the beginning of each month he should give you an advance on the hospital expenses. You see, my dear, everyone used to do it; because it does not suit us otherwise. The money we keep spending is dead money for us,3 do you understand? Do not be upset; look, dear, these words are just suggestions, and then I leave you free to do as you think best. I would not want this to trouble you. The other thing was that you should tell the Bursar that, if he wished, I would send him pears and lint.

  5. Now tell the Manager that I am very eager for a letter from him, since I cannot come for the present. Given the heat and my poor health it would be too great a strain. I assure you that my weakness is extreme; my voice is weak because I am short of breath; I hope that when it gets a little cooler I will be able to set out and be with you.

  1. Then, my dear, here in Piacenza we have the cholera, which is striking hard, and we hope to go to the hospital too. God grant it. On the tenth I will send for Carlottina, because the Director has warned me, on account of the cholera. You see, my dear, how many things there are.4

  2. Tell the Canon too,5 who had promised to write to me but I have seen nothing, that I am eager to have a letter from him, and that he should write; tell him why I am not coming, and not to forget to make a memento for me at Mass, his most unworthy penitent.

  3. What are our dear creatures, the girls, doing now? Are they well? I hope so; and tell my Nunciata6 to be calm and cheerful, for I will write her many things privately. What can I say, it is wretched to know that your letters may be opened; if I did not have this fear, I would write you something funny about Fr. Luigi. He is a canon now; the rest I will tell you in person.

  4. Has Bernardi come back? If he comes, make him pay you; it must be months by now.7 They say that whoever is a fool had better stay at home. Patience! It will serve for another time. What is Fr. Paolo doing? Greet him for me. Likewise Signora Irene, Graziella, the doctor, everyone. Is Giuseppe still angry?

Goodbye, my dear. Likewise my beloved girls, whom I embrace in the Heart of Jesus, and I call myself yours and theirs for ever, Mother Rosa

10. P.S. God bless you and pour into you the true spirit of charity and love towards your neighbour and Jesus. I would send you fruit, but the carriage costs more than the fruit. If you need anything, write and tell me, and I will send you everything.

She teaches her to live in the presence of Jesus, the model of every virtue, and to practise charity like Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

My dear Superior

  1. In my profound nothingness I take up my pen to write to you in reply to your long-awaited letter. I can assure you it was a real consolation to me; but, as you well know,1 my rule is never to rejoice too much in satisfactions, and instead to try to find true joy in the adversities and crosses that Jesus sends us and, as our Master, teaches us.

  2. Yes, my dear, if we want to learn this, we must keep before our eyes this mirror, the figure of the Redeemer, and continually look at our own figure in him. With so true a model, I assure you, everything comes to fit us perfectly.2

  3. Be sure to recommend to your daughters that they keep him always before them, so that they may conform their minds and such sublime [teachings] to true holiness, practising the charity I have so often recommended and which our dear Mother Saint Anne teaches us, a virtue in which she so greatly excelled.3

  4. Ah, dear Superior, I assure you that just writing these two lines about charity, I feel a strong desire in me, and to do what? My God, calm this in me, for it makes me suffer too much. Ah! When will the day come when I can give vent to this great longing of mine?4 What am I doing? Superior, forgive me! But what can I say: when this thought seizes my mind I cannot contain it.

  5. I would have a great many things to say, but I must leave them, because they are waiting for me and I could not resume writing until after lunch, and I am afraid of being judged cruel, as I deserve.5

6. All is well and we are in perfect peace. Everything is falling into place marvellously. I am well; the baths are doing me a great deal of good. Write to me. I recommend that you always keep humble and that you pray, and have others pray, for me to the great Saint, our dear Mother.

Receive, and share with your daughters, your Mother's holy Blessing.

Believe me your Rosa Gattorno6

Report on the conduct of Fr. Luigi Cogrossi at the Mother House.

Most Reverend Excellency,

  1. My conscience would be too uneasy if I did not come, with these ill-connected lines but in all truth, as I have always done in the past, to reveal to you with sorrow the bad conduct of that Priest about whom we had long conversations with Your Excellency more than once.1

  2. Ah! If only I had listened to Your Most Reverend Excellency and made the enquiries that were due;2 but, as if steeped in the most abject ignorance there could be, two years ago I lived in the utmost delusion, until by God's mercy his conduct was revealed almost, one might say, all at once; and now3, as is my duty, I come to give you an account of it, partly written by the complainants themselves (as you will see) and partly by me, concerning the irascibility he showed during the time I had to deal with him more closely in this holy Work of the Lord.

  3. All this, Most Reverend Excellency, I leave in your most prudent hands, that you may make of it the use you wisely make in all your undertakings, confident of a holy and wise outcome, as I have always experienced.

  4. I earnestly beg you to keep my name hidden, and on this I rest easy, knowing Your Most Reverend Lordship's integrity.

I respectfully kiss your hand, sure that I shall have a reply from you to this letter. Asking your blessing, I beg you to believe me Your Most Reverend Excellency's most humble Sr. Anna M. Rosa Gattorno

She reports that Fr. Luigi Cogrossi has been dismissed from the Institute.

Most Reverend Eminence,

  1. With the deepest sorrow I come, in conscience bound, to inform Your Most Reverend Eminence that Cogrossi is no longer part of this poor Institute. Everything was done with the knowledge of the Ecclesiastical Superiors.1

  2. I retract all the enthusiasm and assurances of holiness I ventured to express to Your Most Reverend Eminence. Now, in great sorrow, I must confess my ignorance in never having realised that this man was anything but a Saint, as I saw confirmed by the Holy See (Ecclesiastical) on two occasions.2

  3. I do not dare tell you the reasons now, but if you want any clarification, please apply to my Spiritual Father, whom by God's grace I took as soon as I came to Piacenza and whom Your Eminence will surely know by his reputation and learning: Professor Tornatore, Priest of the Mission at San Lazzaro, brother of the Superior in Rome3 at the College at Montecitorio. He will give you every clarification.

  4. I will only say to Your Eminence that I cannot find words enough to thank the Most High for having preserved the whole Community and me, a very poor creature, from the claws of so ferocious a wolf. We owe all this to our dear Mother Saint Anne, who guarded us so well.

  5. I am sure you will favour me with a reply, in which I know I shall find comfort at so painful a time, assuring me of your prayers for this poor sinner, most unworthy of any good, who deserves only to be reviled and insulted by everyone.

With my forehead to the ground I await your Apostolic blessing, professing myself Your Most Reverend Eminence's most wretched Servant Sr. Anna M. Rosa Gattorno

She tells her that she has dismissed Fr. Luigi Cogrossi. She has sent fruit and other things.

Dear Superior,

  1. Today I received your dear letter together with the Canon's, which, I assure you, came just in time amid the saddest upheavals. I have dismissed Fr. Luigi1 and we no longer have superiors, nor will you ever have them again. Only the Pope and the Bishop will be your Superiors. You are and always will be free. When I arrive I will tell you everything. I can only tell you that I have suffered as it pleased dear Jesus, and I hope this will go towards the remission of my sins. I am still suffering exceedingly, but I am content.

  2. My beloved daughters, dear Superior, God bless you all; I do not and never will cease praying for you, that God may make you Saints, and great Saints. Pray for me. I would go on at greater length in a thousand expressions of the thanks and gratitude I feel towards all of you, but my stomach and the very late hour tonight prevent me.2

  3. The Bursar will receive a sack of pears and a large basket of fruit, which they will divide in three; I have done everything in order, so you need say nothing. I am only letting you know so that you are aware and can act accordingly. I put the Bursar's address on everything; if it should come into your hands, say that it is not yours and have it taken to the Bursar; one of the three shares is for the doctor and the pharmacist, so that you will not be under any obligation to them.3 Inside the sack of pears I put two little parcels for you: the veils, which Rosa will iron, because they had no time here, and stockings for Nunciata.

Goodbye, dear to Jesus and exceedingly dear to me.

Believe me ever your most loving Mother

4. P.S. All four little boots were packed together; the loss must surely have happened on the Railway.

She says she is honoured to correspond with an exemplary person, of deep spirituality and zealous in charity.1

Very Reverend Superior,

  1. Out of obedience2 I set down on this paper some ill-connected characters3 and a few words of comfort, for my wretched tongue [is not] equal to a person such as yourself, whose heart is versed in heavenly sublimities.

  2. I can therefore only raise feeble prayers to the Most High in thanksgiving for such signal benefits, and for leaving here below among us mortals creatures of such exemplary life and learning.

  3. How dear to the Author of all good are the labours, the toil, the tedium of long conversations with people of either sex, from which Your Reverence is accustomed to draw those great benefits that flash like a dream through the mind of this wretched creature; but so great is her misery and so slight her understanding that she cannot make them a subject of discourse.

  4. You surely, O Creator, keep giving me dealings with your beloved creatures, so that this weakened servant of yours may lean on the favourable prayers of these persons, that they may support her and keep her from falling into an abyss of errors.

  5. How glad I was to spend time with a soul who works in the Saviour's vineyard; I can only rejoice and beg you to keep me in a corner of your heart and to believe me, as I truly am, the most unworthy of all creatures.4

Your most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

She thanks her for her reply. She looks forward to her niece joining the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Reverend Superior,

  1. My indisposition, which kept me in bed for some days and from which I have not yet recovered, was the only reason for my delay in thanking you for the pleasure I felt on receiving your most esteemed letter.

  2. Your letter was certainly dear and precious to me; but it pained me just as much to read the title of Superior1 which you give me. I should like to correct you and beg you not to give me that title again, for I am only a poor Daughter of Saint Anne and never a Superior; indeed I live under obedience to the Superior of this House.2

  3. I heard with inexpressible pleasure the news that a dear niece of yours will soon be among my daughters; I cannot express to you the joy I felt, nor can I tell you how eagerly I await her, and the other two as well.3

  4. I thank you for all you are doing for this poor Institute. I am and always will be most grateful to you. Please accept my warmest thanks. Keep me in a corner of your heart, offering fervent prayers to God for me.

Do not forget me, and believe me your most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

She suggests that she ask the hospital Administration for a period of rest in Piacenza for health reasons.

A.M.F.

Good Superior, dear to Jesus, my beloved Superior,

  1. God bless you, dear creature; I cannot find words enough to express to you, with the liveliest feeling of gratitude, what your dear words meant to me. Rest assured that this very poor Mother of yours, as long as she lives, will never cease to pray God to make you holy and grant you everything; when I am dead, if I go to a place of salvation, I will do the same.1

  2. My dear, I am making an effort to write to you in my own hand, which I assure you is tiring for me, because, as you will have heard from this dear Superior, your sister2 — though I would have been far from writing it to you myself — my health is bad. She thought it best [to write and tell you] so that you would know why I have been delayed in coming to Cento.

  3. Dear Superior, I am afraid you are overtiring yourself, and if you think fit to ask the Manager for some help for a time, while you are so burdened with patients, do ask, and if it is granted I will send you a good creature at once and you will be pleased; they will not have to spend anything.3

  4. For charity's sake, write and tell me about the health situation. Is the cholera threatening you at all? If it were, you could let it be known that you would be ready to provide nurses, meaning that I would send them to you from here; you will let this be heard indirectly.4

  5. Dear Superior, what could you ever have done to me? Nothing; I assure you that your words brought tears to my eyes; never write such things to me again; just ask, and you shall have everything.5

  1. As for the collars, if you agree, I will bring them myself, and also the bodice

for Rosa. I sent some that were already begun; if you cannot do them, have the dressmaker finish them; if you want others, I will bring them.6

  1. Dear Superior, what can I say: now I seem to be recovering, but I have my little girl with me and do not know how I can manage to come until her Director calls her back.7 If you would like to come with someone else for the feast of Saint Francis, I could do this: send your sister along with another, good at keeping accounts, for a week, if you like the idea; see whether the Manager would be happy for you to take this holiday, without saying anything. Do you understand? Do as you wish.8

  2. I assure you that when I thought I was dying I thought of you9 and was grieved to leave you without seeing you. And then, the state I was leaving you in! But the good God preserved me, and I hope I will leave you well settled before I die.10 Tell me a little about practical matters. We are well, as Jesus wills; and you? I cannot write any more, for I am suffering a great deal.

Goodbye, dear Francesca, and greet everyone for me. God bless you, and I am for ever your Mother Anna

She has sent fruit and asks for acknowledgement. Expressions of concern and solicitude.

A.M.F.

  1. I have sent you a sack of pears with walnuts, and also a basket for Fr. Paolo. Let me know as soon as you receive them.

  2. I am sorry to learn from the girls' letters that you have lost your voice; for charity's sake take care of yourself, do not fret, because, my dear, you know well that we are in this tearful vale.1 I assure you that suffering, suffering alone, is our inheritance.

  3. Dear, I pray Jesus to give all this to me and relieve all of you. Only to me, because, I assure you, it is very dear to me and I have no other treasure on this earth but suffering. Yes, you are my treasure.2

Goodbye, dear. God bless you all, and drink deep from the cup of suffering.

I am, of our Mother Saint Anne, the most wretched Mother Rosa

They are not to leave Cento. It is better for her to go there.

Dearest Superior,

  1. It is high time I answered your dear letter, which I received the day before yesterday; but if you knew the reason for the delay you would certainly agree with me. You see, hearing that you were preparing to come1 with Eufemia gave me great pleasure, but I could not make up my mind to take your sister2 away from here; and besides, a very vivid thought kept coming to me, and I said to myself, and then spoke of it to the Father3 and the Superior: send a new face down there? You know what sort of people they are; I fear they might take it badly; so I decided to leave the girl and come myself with Caterina.4 That is the decision.

  2. Indeed I will come before you. Everything is happening at once: Countess Castelnuovo,5 whom Anna Maria Rosa knows, is coming on Friday to stay here for several days, so as soon as she leaves I will come.

  3. Pray that the Lord will send me the means to come, for this too is a big obstacle: for four people to go and return it costs 120 [francs]. You see that it is no small expense at a time like this. I assure you it worries me.6 Patience; I would not want to discourage you now that I have confided this to you, but you will take it with patience and resignation, thanking the Lord who wishes to humble us in this way.7

I close, my dear, because my head aches badly.

Receive a handshake from your very poor Mother, as she implores the Lord's holy blessing on you, and I am

your Mother as long as I live, Anna Maria Rosa

She expresses her sorrow over the two sick sisters and gives her spiritual advice and news.

A.M.F.

Dear Superior,

  1. I was intensely grieved to learn that Daria and Eufemia are ill. The Lord wants to humble us in everything. As for a doctor, I would turn to the physician of all our good, our Mother Saint Anne. She will make them well; and then I would give Daria a small spoonful of the oil I left you, and when Eufemia has a nosebleed she should anoint her nose and then say three Our Fathers, Hail Marys and Glory Bes to the Most Holy Trinity.1 Dear Superior, keep me always informed about their health.

  2. Tell me: how are you managing now with the Bursar about money; does he give you an advance? I hope you have done as you were told. Look, my dear, you will see that this poor Mother of yours is giving you good advice; I hope you will not take these words badly.2

  3. If you have in mind to stay and wait for me, I will come as soon as I have taken Carlotta to Milan.3 I will come and stay a long time; and then I think I will come so that you can rest, and you can do as you like: come here or stay near me, making a little retreat, while I do everything with Caterina; are you happy with that?4

  4. Open your heart to me with complete frankness, as I do to you, your very poor mother, who once again feels unwell and is weighed down by the burdens and charges of this poor house.5 Yes, my dear, I recommend you always to keep yourself humbled. Ah! We can never be furnished enough with this [virtue]; and blessed are we if we could be trampled on by everyone! We are never so loved by our Jesus as when, in the world's eyes, we appear useless and despised creatures.6

It is late now and I still have much to write; so, imploring a thousand blessings from Heaven upon you, which I wish the Lord to share among all of you,

I remain ever your Mother Rosa

Letters are going astray. She repeats the recommendations of the previous letter, which did not reach its addressee.

Dear Superior,

1. This is the third letter I have written to you. Now, seeing that they get lost, I have turned to your confessor, without telling him anything, though. I wrote another to the Manager, complaining about this and asking him to look into the matter and see what is going on.1

2. In my last letter I told you to let Daria work. Let her take only Saint Anne as her doctor. Here we have begun the prayers; and I spoke to you about the hundred lire.

3. If you only knew my situation! It is now such that I cannot come. When I arrive I will tell you; be patient.

4. Give me news of Daria and Eufemia; I hope [they are well].

And believe me your most affectionate Mother, imploring for all of you the Holy Blessing from Heaven, to strengthen you in suffering. Forgive me, but sleep is overcoming me, and by day it is almost impossible to write to you.

[your Mother ROSA GATTORNO]

  1. I am sending you the receipt you asked me for.2 It was drawn up by someone who knows about the loan you made to this house. I have copied it out myself and am sending it to you to satisfy your wish.

Dear Teresa,

  1. What can this wretched sinner answer you, lacking words that might bring you, my friend, peace and tranquillity?1 I can only repeat what I have already told you.

  2. You have known my circumstances not just from now but from before there was any talk of your loan to this very poor house.2 I entrust myself to your good judgement and to the will of God, in whom I place everything.

  3. Now, if my Jesus wishes to play with me in this way,3 I bow my head, as to something I deserve. I only pray the Most High to grant this skeleton strength and patience to bear everything in peace.

At the feet of Jesus I call myself your very poor Servant Rosa

My dear Teresa,

  1. I am sorry to keep repeating the same thing to you, for I know very well that I am wearying you.

  2. God knows I would not wish to cause you the slightest annoyance, but what can I do? You know our circumstances and knew them already,1 and you have proof in hand that this house would by no means wish to harm your children, given the good faith in which you placed your trust.2

  3. Since you handed over the money, I reply that it is our wish to repay you as soon as possible.

  4. If you insist and are determined to damage our common cause,3 ignorant of business as I am, I will refer you to my Father, so that he may deal with you as he thinks best.

I am the most wretched Anna Rosa

5. You lent your money to this house of the Lord, and far from refusing, the House is ready to give you the fullest guarantee; so it seems to me this difficulty has been smoothed over, and you can live calm and secure about your children's interests.4 I let you know that on Sunday we have exposition of the Blessed Sacrament.

Goodbye. Greet your Mother for me.5

I am your most unworthy Servant

Rosa

A.M.F.

Dearest Superior,

  1. From your letter, which I found enclosed in one from the Marquis, the Manager,1 I see that all my letters have reached you and none was lost. I think it is your great longing for my letters, so that two days seem like a hundred years to you: so, my dear, that is how it is.

  2. Now I will see to writing a letter to show the Bursar, and then next month he will give you an advance.2

  3. Meanwhile I am sending Fr. Paolo a basket of winter pears, and some to you too. Mention to Signora Irene, I mean in passing, in conversation, to see whether they would be welcome; then, when I send the pears, I would also give some to the Bursar, and take the opportunity to make this remark to him.

  4. I am delighted about our Daria. So I will come without fail at the end of October and stay as long as God pleases.

Greet everyone for me, and try to be the servants of all; of all. I hope you received my letter through the Canon.3 Please greet everyone for me, and I am your Mother Rosa Gattorno

5. P.S. God bless you, dear daughters, and believe me, until eternity, your Mother, your tenderly most loving Mother Rosa.4

She urges her to be generous, sketching the spiritual profile of a Daughter of Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

My dear Superior,

  1. When will the day come when you are a true daughter of our great Mother Saint Anne?1 A daughter of this great woman thinks only of serving her in the office and the place where Jesus has put her, and is attached to nothing and to no one. Why do you always show such attachment to my person and long so much for me to come there? You tell me that by God's goodness things are going well; so is it necessary for me to come a little sooner rather than later?2

  2. On the other hand, my presence is needed here these days for the interests of our Institute and of our Mother Saint Anne. Courage, my daughter, show yourself a generous daughter of our Mother Saint Anne, a daughter detached from everything, a daughter who seeks nothing but the interest, the pleasure and the glory of her Mother, the great Saint. She can accept as daughters only generous hearts who for love of her are ready to go anywhere, stay anywhere, and suffer everything for Jesus.3

  3. As soon as our Mother permits, I will come at once to relieve you, and that will be in a few days, my dear daughter. I hope you will accept what I write as words entirely of our dear Mother Saint Anne, who loves you with all her heart.

  4. As I write to you, your Mother is in the guest quarters with the Superior, your mother and your two sisters, and a little niece. Dear, they are having lunch; you will not believe it: this poor Mother of yours had barely taken a little food and went straight to her desk.

  5. I can hardly write any more. I am exceedingly tired, all day and part of the night.

  6. We have the deaf-mute girls at risk, the hearing girls at risk, and the others.4

  7. Dear, if you could see this poor Mother of yours! I think I must be a skeleton, for judging by the surprise I cause everyone I must be frightening.5 Ah! If only I frightened the devil too, so that when I am dead he will have nothing to do with me.

Tell me about practical matters, and believe me your most loving Mother Rosa

8. I have not yet sent you the pears, but I will soon. Goodbye. Greet everyone for me; I will soon be with you.

She comforts her, speaking of the love of the holy Mother Saint Anne, and gives her spiritual advice. She confides her own worries about the poverty of the Mother House. Other news.

Dear Superior,

  1. Here I am back from Milan, soon to return to [...], where we have taken a house for our Institute.1

  2. Dear to Jesus, be of good heart, for your Mother Saint Anne loves you and takes account of all the sufferings and desolation her Daughter endures, keeping refreshment ready which in due time she will not delay to send you. Now, my dear, is the time to suffer, if one day we want to have a beautiful joy.2 Our father Saint Francis of Assisi used to say: «so great is the good I hope for that every pain is a delight to me». I assure you that if your suffering could be passed on, I would take it all, all of it, on myself, to give you back the happiness you long for. My dear, that happiness is not found among the living on earth but among the living of Eternity, those who tomorrow3 will sing his glories in that blessed abode of Paradise.

  3. As for the great dryness you are suffering, I assure you that if you are resigned, your Mother Saint Anne will console you when you least expect it; and I, your very poor Mother, but full of affection for her daughter Francesca, whom every day she clasps in the heart of her spouse Jesus, to obtain from this wound a true absorption of every earthly thing, that she may come out of it purified by so great a balm.4

  4. My dear daughter, believe this poor Mother of yours, who keeps you always at her side wherever she goes; whatever blessing she receives, she always says to her Jesus: «Beloved of my heart, make this creature wholly holy for me!» And how many things I say to him in the morning, and how many I

have said to him, for my Francesca! Ah, dear daughter, listen: be of good heart and believe that you will soon be comforted.5

  1. As for the bodices,6 I think it better that you buy them if you need them, because, dear Francesca, you see that sending them costs more; and besides, we are now so short of means that I do not know whether I am coming or going.7 Everyone makes fine promises, but when it comes to deeds no one is to be seen. You, who run a small household yourself, can tell me what a sorry business this is.

  2. Dear to Jesus and beloved by me, here we have managed as best we could with rags to protect ourselves from the cold; you see, and always hoping in the Lord's mercy that he will not send cold weather, for I assure you it is a real predicament.8

  3. Now I am soon leaving for this town, where another house is being planted, and then for Milan, where they are already buying a house.9 I cannot stay any longer now, for I have endless things to do.

Pray and have others pray, and receive [the greetings] of one who calls herself with all affection your poor but loving Mother, Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

  1. If you have not yet used the veil I brought you, I would like you to send it back to me, because I need it for Angiola,10 who has to wear a hat, and I could not buy one for now. Soon I will send you a little present for the doctor, to keep his feet warm,11 and something for Graziella; inside I will put some veils, which I assure you are lovely; the ones I told you I had had dyed.

  2. Warm regards to the Manager and to everyone. Dear, about the things I said I would send you, you will say I do not keep my word. It grieves me, but what can I do if we have not bought what you want? I do not speak to you of thrift, for I have had too many proofs of yours, so I know how dear to your heart is your house in Piacenza, so poor and so full of troubles.

Receive an embrace and believe me once again your most loving Mother. Later I will write to Framesta.12 Be so kind as to tell us.

She expresses her sorrow for the Sisters who are suffering from the cold. Let her obtain clothing to protect them. Important news about the Mother House.

A.M.F.

Dear Superior,

  1. A few moments ago I received your dear letter along with two others; I do not know whose they are, because they are not signed.

  2. How sorry I am to hear that you are cold! My Jesus, give them your fire, and they will be warm!1 Dear Francesca, I thought all the quilts were there. If any are missing, tell the Bursar. And besides, don't you all have shawls? Tell the Bursar also to provide you with winter clothes, little jackets, as we had agreed, and the blankets. For charity's sake, wrap up warm!2

  3. Write and tell me in detail what I should bring you for the cold, and I will bring it at once: whether bodices, skirts, whatever you mean; and if you can buy what you want there, do so, and I will be happy.3

  4. Write and tell me whether the Superior of the brothers has come again.4 In a few days I will be with you; but, my dear, what can I say: if you knew how much work there is here, you certainly would not even write asking me to come.

  5. As I told you before, we have begun taking in hearing girls at risk, deaf-mutes, and girls who have already fallen. I have no rest.5 Angiola is studying to become a qualified teacher so that she can do her course; soon we are opening the day schools.6 Dear one of my Jesus, I have also had a lot of trouble with Teresa.7 I will tell you everything when I come. So you see I can say that I am tearing myself away from my labours to please you. Dear, I really do not know whether I am coming or going, I am so immersed in the tangles of this house.

  6. Each time you receive my letters, let me know; have

the shoes I wore last year mended for me. I will bring you the veils and the neckbands,8 and I will let you know the day I leave, because I am making it all one journey. I am going to Milan to take Carlotta and then coming to Cento.9

Greet all my dear daughters for me, and Signora Irene and Graziella too. Caterina sends her greetings, as does the Superior, who is here with me.

Goodbye, and believe me your most loving Mother Rosa

She clarifies her views on the proposals and conditions for the community of Daughters of Saint Anne that was to work for the Patronage for deaf-mute girls in Milan.

Very Reverend Director,

  1. Jesus! What a fine heart you have, to feel so keenly the dangers facing your deaf-mute girls. Ah, how I share your compassion! But for the moment, Director, I cannot tell you to send me the young woman you mention; we shall come to an understanding about that another time.1 Now I reply to the numbered points of your letter.2

  2. On no. 1. I have nothing to object to.3

As to no. 2, I leave it to your kindness to fix the maintenance of my daughters who will come to that house. The Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, in each of its houses, wants no more than its poor food and clothing, and can then work diligently for the glory of God.

On no. 3. I tell you that in that house there cannot be more of my daughters than the Patronage for deaf-mutes wishes, unless4 there were benefactors there who called them to carry out other works of our Institute. This, it is understood, would have to be without any harm to the Patronage itself.

In no. 4 you ask whether I am prepared to stipulate that, in addition to the Patronage's means, the Daughters of Saint Anne should add their own means, if they have any. I reply that the Institute of Saint Anne's Daughters will have, in all its houses, whatever goods benefactors choose to give them, bound by whatever conditions they choose. So you see, Director, that such a question does not arise. If you want to reassure the benefactors about us, tell them that the Daughters of Saint Anne are not servants but mothers, and therefore, as far as it depends on them, they will not only preserve the means of the Patronage entrusted to them but increase them, until, were it possible, the time might come when it could take in the whole world.

On nos. 5 and 6 I have nothing to observe; only, if it were not too presumptuous, I would say that I would not put in the programme the words of no. 5, outings to relatives. Likewise the statement in no. 6 that the deaf-mute girls will go walking in fours. On these points experience may in time teach that it is better done otherwise.5

3. That is what I had to tell you, Director. I hope there is nothing in it to displease you, so that this work may begin, which can do so much good to so many poor deaf-mute girls at risk.6

Please give my most distinguished regards to the esteemed Mistresses7 and believe me Your Reverence's most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

Most esteemed Marchioness,

  1. Your charity and kindness, so well known to me, make me bold to turn to you and ask your help, in a matter very close to my heart, in a need in which I now find myself. I hope and trust that you, who have always been so good to me, will not refuse me your assistance in what I am about to ask, which I dare to hope for only from your great kindness.

  2. Since I am obliged to take up the branch of Deaf-Mute girls at risk, I need a Teacher with a diploma. In our house in Piacenza there is a girl with a good education, received from her very well-to-do family,2 but she lacks the diploma, and to obtain it she needs permission from the Ministry of Public Instruction to sit the examination privately, and also admission to a free place at the Royal Institute in Milan, where there are free places for training as Teachers of the Deaf and Dumb.

  3. Only you, most esteemed Marchioness, through your excellent brother, who has such influence with the Ministry, can obtain these two permissions for me, namely to sit the examination privately and to enter the Institute in Milan, the petition for which I enclose.3

  4. Ah yes, if you could obtain so much through your good offices, be assured that neither I nor my Community could ever forget so great a Benefactress and Co-worker in this work of charity. The many proofs of charity I have received from you encourage me to hope that you will exert yourself for this one too, and I assure you that God will know how to reward you.

Trusting to obtain this, I beg you to accept my most distinguished regards and to believe me your most humble Sr. Anna M. Rosa Gattorno

Very Reverend Director,

1. I am most grateful for the great care Your Reverence takes on my behalf; I must tell you that everything that concerned me, such as my visit to Cento, is done: I am already back.

2. If Your Reverence thinks it best to postpone, do as you please, since I could tell you nothing different from what I have already agreed with Your Reverence.

Kindly convey my most respectful greetings to the honoured Mistresses1 and believe me Your Reverence's

Most humble Sister ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

Dear Superior,

  1. Two lines to keep my word, though they cost me a great deal, as my health is very poor.

  2. Blessed for ever be the will of good Jesus, who gives us such dear suffering.

  3. Let the Marquis, the Manager, know as soon as you can that I am leaving for Milan, having been called by Carlotta's Director to take her back to the School,1 so that if he wanted to come he would not make the journey in vain, as I do not know how long I will stay in Milan.

  4. Tell the daughters to pray for me. Dear Francesca, remember me in the Heart of Jesus, in which I always try to enclose you, and in that dear treasure, the spouse of his beloved ones. Yes, certainly not mine, for I am a sink of sins,2 but yours, blessed Daughters of Saint Anne, our Mother. Surely he will not allow this poor creature to be lost, but will surely let her be converted and die a Christian; God grant it.3

God bless you, and believe me your poor Mother, who loves you tenderly in Jesus

Sr. Anna Maria Rosa

5. P.S. That delivery note you have, which reached you 118

when I was there, was still for the sack of pears you had already received.

Blessed be Jesus

Most esteemed Father Agostino,1

  1. The wine of the Chalice must truly keep you thirsty for you to have so tremendous a burning thirst for it all the time. You are right to long to be inebriated, and I with all affection long to see you drunk with this wine.2

Caterina, my beloved daughter

(I wish no one to see this)

  1. God bless you and arm you with patience; may the mantle of our holy Mother cover you and hide you from the eyes of the world, so that you may not be stolen from Jesus, your beloved Spouse.1

  2. Your sister is no longer coming;2 I wrote the reason to the Superior. Pray for this poor Mother of yours, who is as the Lord wills.

I am your

most loving Mother Rosa

Most esteemed Marchioness,

  1. I received your most esteemed letter; I cannot tell you how pleased I was to hear how you have taken up what I asked of you;2 I assure you that I am and always will be most grateful, and I am certain God will reward you for what you are doing for him.

  2. Good Marchioness, here I am again imploring your kindness to bring this work to completion. A.M.F. My Superior,

  1. Two lines to ask for your news, which I want to hope will be good. Write to me in your own hand, to set my mind at rest.

  2. Listen, my dear: if things go well and I do not have to go to Milan for the Immaculate Conception, I will come to Cento.1 Then we will agree that you call me urgently, and I will come and stay with you for a few days.

  3. But God grant that we may rather have to go to Cerro.2 Pray that Saint Anne, our Mother, will grant this grace, which we need so much.

  4. Dear little daughter, if you knew how serious my troubles are, you would surely pity me, knowing how great is the love you bear this poor Mother of yours, who does not deserve it. A love which, I believe, certainly never departs from the Heart of Jesus, our only good and treasure. Isn't that so?3 My dear Francesca, if you could see this poor Mother of yours, how well she knows how to find you in that Heart! For when she says to Jesus, I entrust my Superior Francesca to you, where am I to put you to rest, if not in the cleft of his Side?4 There alone is found that dear balm that inebriates us.5

  5. I must close, for I feel unwell. I left one thing behind: the image of my Jesus on the bed at Cento. Keep it for me, and I will take it when I come back.

Goodbye; I can do no more, as you will see from the handwriting.

Goodbye; I am your most loving Mother Rosa

Most Illustrious Mayor,

My dear son,

  1. After much suffering I reached Piacenza; I could not send you two lines at once because I was still unwell. Now I am better, and I take the opportunity at once to spend a little time with you.

  2. I hope, my dear Gigino, that by now you have found contentment at school, cared for by your good superiors,1 who will fill the gap left by my departure. So try, dear Gigino,2 to do yourself credit and to see your teachers in the person of the Lord; and so3 love them with all respect and reverence and obey them, for this, dear Gigino, is all you can do to give your poor Mother comfort and joy amid, as you know, so many other irreparable sorrows.

  3. My only comfort will be to hear that you are good, studious and obedient, and I do not want to doubt it. Write to me often; I am still waiting for letters from you. Try to be cheerful, and believe me always

your most loving Mother Rosa

Dear Marchioness,

  1. How welcome was your most esteemed letter of the 3rd of this month, which I would have answered at once, as was my duty, to thank you for so much kindness, but my health prevented me.

I gave your greetings to the Father. Believe me, in the Heart of Jesus, your most obliged friend Rosa Gattorno

A.M.F.

Dear Caterina,

  1. For many days now I have been in perfect health; on the day you left, my dear, I was very ill in the morning and then it all passed; so now I am well, except for my eyes and hands, which still tremble.

  2. Dear Caterina, our separation only increases my affection for you, and I keep saying: what will become of my little daughter? Every moment, and then to our holy Mother: for charity's sake, my Saint Anne, keep for me what you have given me.2

  3. Dear creature, love Jesus and keep him always pressed to your heart; during the day bow your head a little towards your heart and say to Jesus, who is hidden within: my love, I want to be all yours and you all mine, dear Jesus. Another time: my beloved, what are you doing in here alone in so small a dwelling? Ah! speak to me and calm my doubts, confirm me in your love, Jesus my Redeemer, give me your love.3

  4. If I were not afraid this letter might be lost, I would write you many things, but with this fear I will stop. Patience! Jesus will speak for me.

  5. I am in the greatest anxiety, though I do not know what to think: so many days without letters, and I do not even know whether you received mine. Write to me, but above all, come, dear Caterina. That is enough for now.

Goodbye; greet Sr. A. Francesca4 for me, and I am all yours, your poor but most loving Mother, Sr. Anna Maria Rosa

Distressed by Caterina's illness and her Daughters' absence, she asks for news.1

A.M.F.

My dear little Daughters,

  1. What grief I felt on reading Francesca's letter! Even now I find no rest; I keep saying: my God! and then to the Superior: if only I knew whether my Caterina is still in bed!2 What will become of my dear little daughters? My Saint Anne, our Mother, bring them back to me at once, for their absence is too painful for me; the anxious thought is devouring me. Little daughters, hurry, come quickly to the bosom of one who is waiting for you and longs to embrace you affectionately.

  2. My dears, my health has recovered; for two days I have been at the loom, working; only I find writing very hard, and this is the first thing I have written since you left. It seems a century.

  3. Write to me at once with news of Caterina, for I have decided to come and fetch you. Maria is coming on Friday.3 Come, and write to me, and I will come at once; do not leave me in anxiety.

  4. Ah, my little daughters, it is better to stay under mamma's skirts than to travel; poor things, you did it out of obedience, and obedience saved you.4 God bless you and grant that you may always be ready to give your life for this obedience, so as to have heaven for ever.

  5. Pray, as we are praying; tomorrow morning there will be benediction at the holy Mother's altar in thanksgiving,5 that she may soon get my Caterina back on her feet.

I am for ever your most loving Mother, Sr. Anna Rosa

She asks for news and wants them to return as soon as possible.

A.M.F.

My dear Francesca, my daughter,

  1. All you have done is very good; indeed, always do the same, for you, my dear, know the needs of this house.1

  2. I hope you feel better now; but, my Francesca, what grief your letter today caused me! I would have flown into your arms, but an obedience held me back.2

She confides her distress at Caterina's poor health.1

A.M.F.

My dear, beloved little daughter Caterina,

  1. Believe me, this poor Mother of yours shares your suffering and perhaps feels the pain more than you do;2 your absence and the hardships that have befallen you confirm me in deciding that this will be the last time that, as far as I am concerned, you set foot outside without your poor Mother's feet going first.3

  2. My Caterina, as soon as I received Francesca's letter I wanted to fly to you, and I immediately sent the Superior to the Father for permission, but he, fearing for my health, said no. Patience!

  3. Courage, my dear; I hope that by now you are a little better, but to set my mind at rest I am sending you the gardener, because, from what I see, letters are getting lost; I have already written to you twice, and I read in yours that you have received none.

  4. Dear Caterina, our good Jesus wants to test us in every way, but believe me, these trials serve to set the rudder of the boat properly, so that it can sail on without coming to grief.4 Yes, my dear, let us run swiftly along the road of holiness.

  5. My health is excellent; since you left I do not seem the same person: I work, write, embroider, go out5 on foot. I am waiting impatiently for you so that we can go to Milan.

  6. I feel as though I had no arms;6 I go into your room and it saddens me always to see that bed made in the same way. Tomorrow, dear Caterina, my Communion will be all for you, offering it to our dear Mother Saint Anne, because Tuesday is dedicated to her, and this dear Mother will surely heal you. My Angel, Fr. Bernardo, will be a good doctor to you;7 meanwhile I am sending you the cigars,8 though I know that by now you will not need them any more, and the oil too.9

7. Come soon, and send me good news, which I am impatiently awaiting; I have many things to tell you, but I will tell you them all in person.

Goodbye, my dear; receive a thousand blessings from one who loves you dearly, who calls herself your poor but ever most loving

Mother Rosa

Most esteemed Madam,

  1. It is a long time, dear Marchioness, since I had news of you; I would have liked to ask you the reason sooner, but as I could not do so in my own hand, I refrained.

  2. Now I really want to venture to put together two ill-connected lines to tell you how much this most wretched creature always feels she owes you in thanks and gratitude for all you have done, of which I shall keep an eternal memory.2

Very Reverend Canon,

He has helped the work for the little orphan girls with fatherly interest and brought them joy. Let him send the two looms and continue to help them as he can, for their number has grown greatly.1

Most Illustrious Mayor,

  1. The last time I had the pleasure of seeing you, I would have liked to tell you a great many things about the work which Your Lordship, with a truly fatherly affection, has begun for these unfortunate creatures; but the surprise of the welcome you gave these little girls of yours prevented me, their poor wretched Mother, from telling you of the thousand needs of these daughters of yours; so great was the joy these innocent souls felt that I cannot keep from you this fact: after lunch, when I went to their recreation, they all said to me joyfully: we have seen our good Father!

  2. You spoke of sending me a loom, mentioning that you had two of the same kind.2 I now beg your kindness to send me both, together with a craftsman able to set them up; I am sure you will grant this request, which is entirely for the good of your daughters.

  3. Now, as I also mentioned to you, you would need to give some subsidy, because the number is large, as you saw, and keeps growing.

  4. For my part I do not and will not fail to do all I humanly can, as their most wretched Mother, to help them; but you, as a father, must come to their aid, thinking that one day you will have honour from the world for it, glory from God, and the affection of these dear creatures, who will love you for ever; and when, grown older just enough to be able to support themselves, we will put your plan into effect.

5. I am sure you will see a work that will suit you. So think about it and help me, because there are no longer twelve or thirteen girls to keep, but twenty-five.

Confident that you will send me a couple of lines of comfort, which I anxiously await, I sign myself Your Lordship's

Sr. Rosa Gattorno

Most Illustrious President,

  1. I received your most esteemed letter, regarding which2 I cannot conceive how the Hospital can expect this3 Institute to secure a young woman's future for 200 francs; moreover, in this poor Institute only annual vows are made; so, Most Illustrious President, please understand that it is my intention that whenever4 she has to leave for any reason, she is to be taken back by her own House.

  2. It seems to me that I have done more than could be done for any other girl, since she was accepted purely as a favour, these conditions being inadmissible for us.5

  3. She therefore remains free in the mission, because the expenses needed for her profession already far exceed this small sum.6

I ask you for a reply, to console a creature who longs for it so much.

most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

Most Illustrious Manager,

  1. I was extremely grieved to hear that two of the nurses are ill.2 I would gladly have flown to them to bring them some relief, but my frail health, which has kept me in bed with fever for several days, prevents me.

She informs him, regarding a postulant who had left the Institute, of what happened about the financial arrangements made for her.12

Very Reverend Father,

1. Here I am to tell you everything that has happened since Paola3 ceased to belong to this poor Institute.

She asked to enter the Daughters of Saint Anne through a Lady, out of regard for whom I accepted her4 without the dowry required of everyone.

  1. To make up at least a small sum on entering, she also brought a little gold, which I said I did not want and should be sold. Indeed, in the presence of this Lady5 and other persons, she handed over the gold, which a third person sold for 68 francs. After entering she gave me a few other things, which I returned to her when she left; and of the whole sum of money she gave me, including the gold worth 68 francs, I received 368 francs.

  2. When she left,6 it seemed to me that I had settled her account conscientiously. Then, after several months, she began to trouble me; then she stopped and was silent for I do not remember how many months. Again she wrote furiously; I replied; and again she was silent for some months; then she had a Priest write to me again.7 I replied to this Priest that I was sending her a money order for 20 francs, for fear, as she wrote, that there might be a loss on the exchange,8 since I had settled her account in notes and not in gold, as she had told me.

  3. Some time later the Priest wrote that she would not accept the money order but wanted more. I then set out my reasons to him by letter, sending him Paola's account in detail and assuring him that his belief that that

Lady had given me money for her was untrue.9

5. After this I received no further reply. A year has passed since then, and now, when I almost thought she no longer existed, the Priest sent me back10 the 20-franc money order without a word of explanation. That is all that happened to her in this house.11

Believe me, with all esteem and respect, Your Reverence's most humble Sr. Anna M. Rosa Gattorno

She encourages her to follow Jesus on the way of suffering. The cross is the pledge of every joy.

A.M.F.

My dear Daughter Francesca,

  1. Courage! Why, now that we are on the mountain, do we lose heart at the crucifixion? Ah, no! Rather, we must prepare for the executioners the nails of our tribulations and long for them to be driven in soon.1

  2. Come, my dear, courage, for good Jesus will soon console you; he has already begun, but let us not settle for sweets, no!2 Let us always remember that he was not given holy wine, but gall and vinegar; so if we are to follow him, there is nothing for us but to suffer, suffer.3 Long live suffering! Dear daughter,

  1. I gladly carry your little cross, provided that you are left perfectly free. I am sorry that it is not for me to take it from you, because the only one that troubles you, you must remove yourself.1

  2. You will have understood me: trust me more, break down the wall of shyness, come to me with your heart on your lips. That is the cross you feel without relief.2 Come like a little child — yes, my daughter —; you want to, but what prevents you? Shyness! Ah, no, my dear, overcome this silliness, because, you see, it is a worldly perfume;3 but from pouring out one's heart into the breast of a spiritual mother, one gains from such sharing only pleasant things and heavenly consolations.4

  3. Jesus said: When there are two who speak of me, I will be in their midst.5

Love me and believe me your poor

Mother Rosa. Burn this at once6

How to respond to the love of Jesus.

A.M.F.

Caterina, my little daughter,

  1. If you knew how much Jesus loves you! You would surely be mad about him and do nothing but press him to your heart and say to him: My love, speak to me, command me, for I want to do everything that pleases you. Yes, my little daughter, you will feel it if you follow his will and his voice, and you will see that he himself will console you with love and caresses.1 Then you will say: Ah! what my spiritual mother told me was true, and she did everything for my good, an infinite good! Then you will leave the flesh behind and feel repugnance for it.2

  2. Write me two lines of comfort, confirming you in your state.

  3. Love, love Jesus, for in him you will find everything you desire: pleasure, delight, love, caresses, and food, drink and rest as well. Goodbye; you will see why I do not write more. Sr. A. Adelaide4 will tell you.

Having arrived to open the new work, she and the Sisters of the new community have been warmly welcomed by the local people. She expresses her distress at being a cause of suffering to the Sisters of the Piacenza community and asks pardon of the Superior and the community. She adds news and greets everyone.1

A.M.F.

Dearest Superior,

  1. After a good journey and a most happy arrival,2 and today a magnificent day, heaven is celebrating for us and seems to echo the people's cheers;3 my God, only this servant of yours is immersed in every kind of tribulation and tastes nothing of all the relief and contentment nature offers her.

  2. Everything, my dear, only serves to heap suffering upon suffering for me, for I am now at the height of tribulation without the least relief;4 where I might find it, I do not want it — yes, my dear, spiritual and temporal, of course; and yet it is curious (let me put it this way): I find here a great many spiritual lions who want nothing more than to listen to me, and I have to struggle to get away, because they are deluded; but if they had to live with me and hear of my infamies, their hunger would certainly pass, and from wolves they would become wild beasts that would flee from me at the mere sound of my voice.5 Patience; only the Lord's mercy can save this wretch.6

  3. Ah! my dear, if you knew how agonising it is for me to think that I am your ruin, your scandal, that I serve only to ruin the Lord's Work; I feel my insides torn apart, and I keep thanking my God for having taken me out and sent me far from you; and so you will be able to receive more abundant providence from heaven, without this most infamous creature holding it back; and so your hearts will receive from the hand of the holy Mother (alas, that I dare call Mother her to whom I can bring nothing but outrage) gifts, spiritual graces and light to keep the holy book of the Rules well.7 My God, what will become of wretched me? Pray, for charity's sake, that I may not be lost.8

  1. As I write to you I am at Fr. Ricchini's house,9 for we are spending the whole day here today. Imagine the poor wretch with the sentence on her back of being able to eat nothing but bread: what a blush, what shame, what suffering!10 And besides, I am enormously swollen; but I feel nothing beyond the usual; if only I did not have the agonising pain of this word ringing in my ears, that I am so infamous and, moreover, your damnation. And yet, my dear, I can assure you that in all this wretch has done and said, her thought was always for your good, and a thousand times I neglected myself for your good; and yet, yes, there are those who say that I am your ruin.11 My God, my very heart! Why did you not bring me out of this blindness sooner? Ah! I would not have mishandled the affairs of my conscience so badly and would be less unhappy.

  2. Dear Luigia, forgive me for everything I have done to you and obtain the same forgiveness for me from the community; and I will live, as you see, unhappy, deprived of all help, even human, fighting painfully as long as it pleases my God.

  3. Add to this that I am among such good creatures, to whom God has given the grace of behaving so well and even being affectionate, that — apart from the caresses, for you know well I am as rough as can be and do not much care for them — as for the rest, I assure you, they only stir up sorrow in me.12

  4. I do not know when I will come, because there is a question here of buying a very large building, two or three times the size of the one in Piacenza, and since last night they have been telling me they do not want me to leave until after the Christmas feasts; they want everything settled first.13 Greet everyone for me.

  5. Last night, as soon as we arrived, we got down at the church door; the candles on the altars were lit and the Te Deum was recited with various prayers to the Immaculate Conception and Saint Anne. When we had gone indoors we stayed talking until 2 in the morning.

  6. Goodbye; greet all your daughters and believe me your most unhappy mother, wretched and full of sorrow. I would still like to tell you something, but Fr. Ricchini is here and I am afraid of boring him. Two hurried lines to Carlotta; I hope to send for her soon, since I have to stay so long.

Goodbye; I am your most loving Mother, Sr. Anna Maria Rosa

Most Illustrious President,

  1. What a blow I received today! As I was arriving from Genoa, in the joy of a new foundation of Nurses,2 I received the painful wound of the good Manager's letter announcing so sad a fact.3

  2. My God! You know well whether there can be any fault to deserve such condemnation; but if man has no other justice than that of his false opinion, let the divine will be done in us, and God, who is truth and most perfect justice in himself, will do justice to the oppressor.

  3. Forgive me, then, good President, if my words are too vehement; but take them as dictated by grief, for I cannot quiet my mind and give it a satisfying reason.4 I am sure I shall find one in your immense charity and in a reply from you, for I have always found you a good protector and defender, as I have so often experienced in similar cases.

  4. Do not, then, leave in so sad a position one who is sure to find in your noble heart words of comfort and good hope. Please give my most heartfelt and cordial greetings to your most honourable wife, and speak a word of justice too, knowing how your heart beats for the good of others.

Accept the sentiments of esteem and respect of one who has the honour to call herself Your Lordship's most humble Rosa Gattorno

My dear daughter,

  1. What troubles, my dear! As soon as I arrived I received the most painful news: the Sisters at Cento are being driven out for ever, the reason being that they do not want nuns;1 you can imagine the wound this grieving heart received. Patience! I wrote at once, and tomorrow, though still swollen, I leave for Cento.

  2. Pray and have others pray; say nothing to anyone. Angiola2 is still ill, and today the doctor told her to take care of herself; but she hopes in the Lord's mercy that she will soon recover, and then she will come with the teacher.

  3. For charity's sake, my Francesca, try to make as much of that person3 as you can, because, if you only knew, our whole future depends on her; so strength, courage and patience for love of Jesus. This thought is enough to bear everything gladly, for in this way we please dear Jesus, and the Most High will not fail to console you soon.

  4. Dear daughter, I close because it is very late, having written to the Monsignor of Genoa and to Fr. Ricchini, as he will tell you. For your guidance, tell him to rest easy, for I have written to the Bishop and all will be in order and turn out well; you did right to answer him as you did today. We have sent the Rules to be printed, but they cannot be finished until the end of January.4

■^ Hospital at Cento. The courtyard.

  1. My Francesca, be patient if I cannot take you away at once;5 but rest assured that this poor Mother of yours left you in body but took you away in spirit, to enclose you continually in the Heart of Jesus, so that in a true fusion of love you may forget this wretch and seek to find and see her only in the bosom of the Eternal Father.

  2. Yes, my dear, for charity's sake, even if God gave me a hundred years of life I could never forget the care you gave this wretched creature. Rest assured that I will always have a greater degree of affection for you, out of pure gratitude for the care you gave me; and may God bless you and pour out his graces on you in torrents, so that you may become a true Daughter of Saint Anne; I do not mean that you are not one now, but I want you to be something more.6

  3. Goodbye, dear Francesca; pray and have others pray that I may settle the battle going on there.

Greet all the others for me and tell them I wish them a thousand blessings from heaven.

I am your most loving Mother, Sr. A. M. Rosa

My dear daughter,

My dear, beloved daughter,

  1. Blessed be the hand that deigns to strike us; I am at Cento, as you see from the date, amid ugly battles.1 Only God can give us victory; prayer is our only shield. My health is the same as ever, except that I suffered nothing on the journey, which was very happy. It is truly the devil's great carnival time;2 but this, my dear, should console us, because it makes us sure that as long as he keeps making efforts and battles it means he is still angry and meets only defeat; so this infernal enemy will be left ugly and humiliated, on our account.

  2. The swelling of my face is the same as when I left you. This morning I could not get up early because of those very bad pains in my shoulders. I hope in the Lord's mercy that he will not give me more for now, so that I will not have to stay in bed. I assure you this thought distresses me greatly, but trust in the divine mercy overcomes everything.

  3. I hope Fr. Ricchini has received my letter and calmed down,3 and I hope too that the letter I wrote to the Monsignor will do the work good.

  4. The Rules are being printed with full approval;4 you can reply to me here, as I will stay another week or perhaps longer.

  5. I hope you will soon have Angiola and the teacher with you.5 Do well, and try, for charity's sake, to make much of the person you know;6 all this, for love of our Jesus, we must suffer everything patiently.

  1. Soon I will try to replace you; I obtained permission from the Father,7 but, as you see, present circumstances prevent me from doing what I would like and what is needed, even the most necessary; I have to stay here sequestered and anxious, unable to do anything, and yet Piacenza needs me there, and I also need to come to you soon to finish settling everything. I hope Ricchini will be satisfied, and the other person too.8

  2. Write and tell me whether you have received 50 francs from Papa, and press him about the beds. Try to make all the straw mattresses, because when I come I will bring Domenica,9 if it pleases the Lord that things are settled. Try to persuade the teacher to have the decoction rubbed on her chest with a little massage;10 it seems to me we are not short of vocations.

Greet Gesuina and Serafina for me.11 God bless you, and you, my dear, receive a thousand blessings from heaven, which this very poor Mother of yours implores for you, calling herself in the Heart of Jesus your most loving Mother Rosa

8. P.S. Do not write about matters of conscience, because here our letters are inspected.

Tribulations accepted in faith produce spiritual consolations and win us the strength to forgive those who offend us. Prudence in speaking with people outside the house, and inside it too, about Cento.

A.M.F.

Dear Daughter and Superior,

  1. I, your very poor mother, want to spend some time today answering your letter too. I picture myself amid your dear delights, but because of my wickedness I must go without them:1 after sins, penance is needed! Blessed hand of my God, I kiss you a thousand times as I feel you pressing on my back.2

  2. Yes, daughter of Saint Anne, let us rejoice amid tribulations, our only pledge and comfort. Ah! blessed the soul that knows how to rejoice in tribulation and receives the blows of divine justice with relish and consolation.3 This is the only way to calm this spoiled humanity of ours, always ready to rebel against those who offend it.4

  3. You tell me we have many enemies. What consolation I felt on reading this! I am only sorry to see you still so anxious and taking these things too much to heart. I would like you to pay less attention to them and be at least indifferent.5 Only be very careful when you have to speak with people from outside, whether men or women, but no dealings at all, however slight; always on the alert; and in the house too never say anything, especially about what you know concerning things here.6

  4. Nothing new; we just have to pray. Last night I was with Daria. What little sleep I had was very little;

I was happy; she held me in her lap. It is a dream, and Carlotta says: those are fibs.7

5. As for what you asked me, I wrote everything to the Father. He will tell you how to proceed. It is half past four and I still have to say all my prayers.8 I will say no more, because I want to go to the Chapel.

Goodbye, my dear; God bless you, and I am your most loving Mother Rosa9

My dear, dear daughter,

  1. I returned from Cento on the 10th, after suffering immensely, and alone. Never again will I let myself be left alone.

  2. My dear, it seems the Lord wants to confirm our sisters in this Hospital; God grant it! What can I say?   3. Courage, my dear; after New Year's Day, if you want me to come, I will come before the boarding and day schools for boys begin. You will call me by letter,2 and Fr. Ricchini too; Angiola will tell you the rest in person.3

Amid the cross of the sisters' illnesses, patience and courage are needed.

My dear daughter Francesca,

  1. Two hurried lines, as I am not very well and have to work on so many pressing matters. I have just received your letter, in which I learn with sorrow that all of you are ill, especially Angiola, whose illness I hear is so stubborn that the doctor must be called.

  2. Patience, my dear, courage; you know well that the enemy wants to play his part in this house at Genoa;1 having no other obstacles or ways to torment us, he torments us with illness; he began with me and keeps on.

  3. Courage, everything will be put right, because this ugly monster will never win again; his efforts are useless. Let us hope in the Lord's mercy.2

  4. My dear little daughter, you call me, and you know well how gladly I am with you, but because of my duties here I cannot come for the moment. Write and keep me informed about everyone's health, especially those who are worst.

Today the Christmas novena began; unite yourself with this wretched Mother of yours,3 who will hold you tight in the Child Jesus, so that my dear little daughter may learn always to be little,4 to grow only in spirit and in the love of her Spouse and be wholly consumed in him. I, wretched as I am, will try to offer your prayers together with mine, that Jesus may console you amid your cross.

Goodbye;

I am your most loving Mother Rosa

My Caterina, dear to Jesus,
